facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Narration centers on Wendy’s realization about growing up and identifies the family as the Darlings (Wendy came first, then John, then Michael).

facts.text: Attends Miss Fulsom's Kindergarten, escorted by Nana.
facts.argument: "the three of them going in a row to Miss Fulsom's Kindergarten school, accompanied by their nurse"

facts.text: In her imagined Neverland, Wendy lived in a house of leaves deftly sewn together and kept a pet wolf forsaken by its parents.
facts.argument: "Wendy in a house of leaves deftly sewn together. ... Wendy had a pet wolf forsaken by its parents."

facts.text: Matter-of-factly claims Peter visits her at night to play his pipes at the foot of her bed; insists he is not grown up and 'just my size' (mind and body), and thinks he enters by the window.
facts.argument: 'It is so naughty of him not to wipe his feet'… 'sat on the foot of her bed and played on his pipes'… 'he isn't grown up… just my size'… 'I think he comes in by the window.'

facts.text: Tidy by nature; scolds Peter (lightly) for not wiping his feet when she finds leaves in the nursery.
facts.argument: "It is so naughty of him not to wipe his feet… She was a tidy child."

facts.text: Play-acted as her mother during a make-believe reenactment of her own birth, dancing with joy at the 'news.'
facts.argument: "playing at being herself and father on the occasion of Wendy's birth" … "Wendy had danced with joy."

facts.text: She quickly fetched her father's medicine and believed his claim that he bravely took nastier medicine as a boy.
facts.argument: "I'll bring it"; she returned "as quick as I could" and believed his childhood claim.

facts.text: Showed practical leadership and compassion: proposed a simultaneous medicine-taking to resolve the standoff, expressed dismay when her father cheated, and comforted Nana by hugging her.
facts.argument: "Why not both take it at the same time?"; "O father!"; "Wendy hugged Nana."

facts.text: Recognizes Nana’s distinct bark for danger and correctly identifies it this night.
facts.argument: Wendy: "That is not Nana's unhappy bark... that is her bark when she smells danger."

facts.text: Her full name is Wendy Moira Angela Darling.
facts.argument: “Wendy Moira Angela Darling,” she replied with some satisfaction.

facts.text: Sews Peter’s shadow onto his foot using her housewife (sewing bag), showing practical, motherly skill.
facts.argument: “It must be sewn on” … “she got out her housewife [sewing bag], and sewed the shadow on to Peter’s foot.”

facts.text: Adopts a patronising, motherly tone toward Peter, calling him “dreadfully ignorant” and “my little man.”
facts.argument: “‘You’re dreadfully ignorant.’ … ‘I shall sew it on for you, my little man,’ she said.”

facts.text: Gives Peter a thimble as a “kiss,” receives an acorn button as his “kiss,” and wears it on a chain around her neck; it later saves her life (narrator foreshadowing).
facts.argument: She gives him a thimble; he gives her an acorn button, which she says she’ll wear on a chain. Narrator: “It was lucky that she did put it on that chain, for it was afterwards to save her life.”

facts.text: Wendy kisses Peter and receives a 'thimble' in return; she understands Peter confuses kisses and thimbles and is flattered by Peter's views on girls.
facts.argument: She says, "so you may give me a kiss," then kisses him; Peter "thimbled" her; she is flattered when Peter says girls are too clever to fall out of prams.

facts.text: Wendy agrees to go with Peter, but only if John and Michael can come and be taught to fly.
facts.argument: "Peter, would you teach John and Michael to fly too?" "If you like," he said, and she ran to wake her brothers: "Peter Pan has come and he is to teach us to fly."

facts.text: Wendy is excited at the prospect of seeing mermaids.
facts.argument: "Oh," cried Wendy, "to see a mermaid!"

facts.text: Experienced her first flight after Peter blew fairy dust, expressing delight.
facts.argument: After Peter "blew some on each of them," she joined the mid-air chorus: "Oh, lovely! ... Look at me!"

facts.text: Can now fly strongly but remains somewhat clumsy, tending to kick too much and bump into clouds when trying to avoid them.
facts.argument: "They could now fly strongly... the more they tried to avoid [a cloud], the more certainly did they bump into it."

facts.text: Prefers ‘tea first’ over immediate adventure when frightened.
facts.argument: “Wendy said ‘tea first’ quickly.”

facts.text: Shudders and whispers in fear asking who resists their landing.
facts.argument: “Wendy whispered, shuddering, ‘Who are they?’”

facts.text: Arrived flying overhead and was shot in the breast by an arrow from Tootles (after Tinker Bell's incitement), falling to the ground.
facts.argument: "Wendy was now almost overhead... then he fired, and Wendy fluttered to the ground with an arrow in her breast."

facts.text: Wore Peter’s button—his ‘kiss’—on a chain around her neck; it deflected Tootles’s arrow and saved her life, though she remains in a frightful faint.
facts.argument: “See… the arrow struck against this. It is the kiss I gave her. It has saved her life.”; “being still in a frightful faint”

facts.text: Among the Lost Boys she is called “the Wendy lady.”
facts.argument: “the Wendy lady lives.”

facts.text: While sleeping, Wendy sings and describes the kind of house she wants (the littlest house with red walls, mossy roof, gay windows, roses, and babies peeping out).
facts.argument: She "began to sing" in her sleep: lyrics describing the house features.

facts.text: Accepts the role of mother to the Lost Boys, agreeing to care for them.
facts.argument: "O Wendy lady, be our mother." ... "Very well," she said, "I will do my best."

facts.text: Promises to put the boys to bed and finish the story of Cinderella, reinforcing her motherly storyteller role.
facts.argument: "Come inside at once... before I put you to bed I have just time to finish the story of Cinderella."

facts.text: Slept in the little house the first night while the boys took the great bed below, and she quickly grew to love the home under the ground; she fitted her hollow tree on the first try.
facts.argument: "she herself slept that night in the little house... And how ardently they grew to love their home under the ground; especially Wendy." / "Wendy... fitted their trees at the first try"

facts.text: Runs the underground household almost constantly—stringing lines for washing and cooking both real and make‑believe meals for the boys—often remaining below ground for weeks.
facts.argument: “Wendy stretched strings… suspended her washing… Really there were whole weeks when… she was never above ground. The cooking… even if there was no pot… she had to keep watching…”

facts.text: Acts as full-time mother in the underground home, managing washing and cooking (often make‑believe) and sometimes staying below ground for weeks.
facts.argument: “Really there were whole weeks when… she was never above ground. The cooking… even if there was no pot… she had to keep watching…”

facts.text: Wendy spends late-night “breathing time” after the others sleep sewing and darning for the boys—reinforcing worn knees—and, worried about their fading memories, she sets examination papers about their parents to keep the old life in mind (which all the boys join).
facts.argument: “her favourite time for sewing and darning was after they had all gone to bed… putting double pieces on the knees… What did disturb her… John remembered his parents vaguely… Michael… willing to believe she was really his mother… she tried to fix the old life in their minds by setting them examination papers… The other boys… insisted on joining.”

facts.text: She feels at ease about her parents because she is sure they keep the nursery window open for her return, so she does not worry about them.
facts.argument: “she was absolutely confident that they would always keep the window open for her to fly back by, and this gave her complete ease of mind.”

facts.text: Wendy is beginning to forget details of home and her mother while in Neverland.
facts.argument: “the questions were all written in the past tense… What was the colour of Mother’s eyes… Wendy… had been forgetting, too.”

facts.text: Enforces strict routines for the children: bedtime by seven and a mandatory rest after the mid-day (even make-believe) meal; she often sits stitching while supervising them.
facts.argument: “strict rules about every one being in bed by seven”; “Wendy insisted on their… half an hour after their mid-day meal… even though the meal was make-believe… She was very busy, stitching.”

facts.text: As a young mother she bravely let the boys sleep despite sensing danger and hearing muffled oars, revealing maternal inexperience and courage; she cried at witnessing her first tragedy.
facts.argument: "she would not waken them... Even when she heard the sound of muffled oars... she did not waken them... Was it not brave of Wendy?" and "Wendy was crying, for it was the first tragedy she had seen."

facts.text: Prudent and protective; moved to cover Peter’s mouth to stop his crow so he wouldn’t betray them, and felt proud when Hook said the boys had found a mother.
facts.argument: "her hand went out to cover his mouth"; she "swelled with pride" at "those boys have found a mother."

facts.text: Exhausted and unable to reach the island alone, Wendy offers to draw lots but is sent away by Peter using Michael's kite; she clings to him and resists leaving before being pushed off to safety.
facts.argument: "Do you think you could... without my help?" She admits she is too tired. She suggests drawing lots; Peter ties the kite tail around her and pushes her off.

facts.text: She enforced bedtime after the boys returned hours late, then was tender the next day, handing out bandages so they could play at limping and slings.
facts.argument: “Great were the rejoicings… they were several hours late for bed… Wendy… cried, ‘To bed, to bed’… Next day… she… gave out bandages… and they played… at limping… and carrying their arms in slings.”

facts.text: Enforces strict mealtime etiquette during make-believe teas: no hitting back, and disputes must be raised by lifting the right arm and saying, "I complain of so-and-so"; she insists on silence when all talk at once.
facts.argument: "There was a fixed rule... should refer the matter... by raising the right arm... saying, 'I complain of so-and-so';" "'Silence,' cried Wendy..."

facts.text: Continues motherly housekeeping: makes the boys clear away, sits to sew a pile of holed stockings, and insists on keeping someone in a cradle (choosing Michael as the littlest).
facts.argument: She tells them to clear away, then sews stockings; to Michael: "I must have somebody in a cradle... and you are the littlest."

facts.text: Relishes domestic evenings by the fire with Peter and the boys; in make-believe, she considers them a large family and says she has ‘passed her best,’ seeking reassurance Peter won’t exchange her.
facts.argument: “There is nothing more pleasant… to rest by the fire with the little ones near by.”; Wendy: “with such a large family… I have now passed my best… you don’t want to change me, do you?”

facts.text: She tells a recurring good-night story about her parents, Mr. and Mrs. Darling, which the boys love and Peter hates.
facts.argument: "for Wendy's story, the story they loved best, the story Peter hated"; "The gentleman's name... was Mr. Darling, and her name was Mrs. Darling."

facts.text: She champions a mother’s love in her storytelling, asserting that mothers leave windows open and imagining a future where she and her brothers return home to their parents.
facts.argument: “the mother would always leave the window open”; “Can they be John and Michael?... So up they flew to their mummy and daddy.”

facts.text: Resolves to return home at once, fearing "perhaps mother is in half mourning"; she clutches her brothers and sharply asks Peter to make the necessary arrangements.
facts.argument: "'Wendy, let's go home' ... 'At once' ... 'Perhaps mother is in half mourning by this time' ... 'Peter, will you make the necessary arrangements?'"

facts.text: Wendy enjoys administering 'medicine' (really water) to the boys, shaking the bottle and counting the drops.
facts.argument: "She loved to give them medicine... Of course it was only water... she always shook the bottle and counted the drops."

facts.text: Wendy habitually tucked the children inside the coverlet at night, believing they might grow chilly toward the turn of the night.
facts.argument: "she had always tucked them inside it, because you never know that you may not grow chilly at the turn of the night."

facts.text: In times of Peter's distress, she customarily lifted him from bed to her lap to soothe him, returning him before he fully woke.
facts.argument: "it had been Wendy's custom to take him out of bed and sit with him on her lap, soothing him... and ... put him back to bed before he quite woke up."

facts.text: Captured by the pirates; bound and held aboard their ship.
facts.argument: "Wendy bound, and on the pirate ship"

facts.text: She would leave her handkerchief at an important place as a clue for rescuers.
facts.argument: "Wendy would leave her handkerchief at some important place."

facts.text: On the Jolly Roger, Wendy showed scorn for the pirates’ filth—writing 'Dirty pig' on grimy portholes—and delivered steadfast 'last words' urging the boys to die like English gentlemen.
facts.argument: "No words of mine can tell you how Wendy despised those pirates." ... "there was not a porthole... 'Dirty pig'; and she had already written it on several." ... "We hope our sons will die like English gentlemen."

facts.text: Wendy was tied to the Jolly Roger’s mast by Smee during the pirates’ execution preparations.
facts.argument: "It was Smee who tied her to the mast."

facts.text: Wendy, bound to the mast, alone dared face the cabin door watching for Peter; after Peter freed her bonds, she concealed herself as he took her place.
facts.argument: "Yes, one, Wendy ... watching for the reappearance of Peter"; "who all this time had been bound to the mast"; "Peter cut Wendy's bonds ... whispered for her to conceal herself"

facts.text: Stayed out of the fight; afterward praised the boys equally, put them to bed in the pirates' bunks, and comforted Peter when he cried in his sleep.
facts.argument: "Wendy... had stood by taking no part... She praised them equally... got them to bed... He... cried in his sleep... and Wendy held him tightly.

facts.text: Wendy is aboard the Jolly Roger during the return voyage, the lone “woman aboard.”
facts.argument: “There was a woman aboard.” Context links this to Wendy, who is sewing Peter a new suit in the same passage.

facts.text: She is on the return voyage to the mainland/home with Peter and the boys.
facts.argument: “turned the ship round, and nosed her for the mainland… we venture into that familiar nursery only because its lawful occupants are on their way home.”

facts.text: Aboard the ship, she and her brothers are planning a surprise return home, expecting to arrive 'Thursday week' and anticipating their parents' reactions.
facts.argument: "They have been planning it out on the ship... the children are coming back... they will be here on Thursday week... mother's rapture, father's shout of joy, Nana's leap..."

facts.text: Currently flying home to the Darling house; within two miles of the window.
facts.argument: “They are really within two miles of the window now, and flying strong.”

facts.text: Feels her first real remorse for leaving home and devises a gentle plan to reveal their return by slipping into their beds.
facts.argument: "with her first real twinge of remorse... 'Let us all slip into our beds, and be there when she comes in.'"

facts.text: Returns home to No. 14 and reunites with her parents, embracing her mother as the family wakes and gathers.
facts.argument: "Mother!" ... Mrs. Darling stretched out her arms... they went round Wendy and John and Michael; she called, "George, George!" and Mr. Darling woke; Nana came rushing in.

facts.text: By arrangement with her mother, Wendy may visit Peter for one week each year to do his spring cleaning.
facts.argument: "Mrs. Darling... made this handsome offer: to let Wendy go to him for a week every year to do his spring cleaning."

facts.text: Mrs. Darling frames the annual spring-cleaning visit as an offer to Peter rather than a concluded arrangement.
facts.argument: "she made this handsome offer: to let Wendy go to him for a week every year to do his spring cleaning."

facts.text: Desired a more permanent arrangement with Peter and asked him not to forget her before spring cleaning time.
facts.argument: "Wendy would have preferred a more permanent arrangement... 'You won't forget me, Peter, will you, before spring cleaning time comes?'"

facts.text: Wendy grew up willingly, married (in white with a pink sash), and had a daughter named Jane; she now tells Jane bedtime stories when the nurse has her evening off.
facts.argument: “Wendy was married in white with a pink sash… Years rolled on again, and Wendy had a daughter… Once a week Jane’s nurse had her evening off; and then it was Wendy’s part to put Jane to bed.”

facts.text: She liked to grow up and chose to do so a day earlier than other girls; as a girl she tried to avoid growing pains for Peter’s sake and felt untrue to him when winning a prize for general knowledge.
facts.argument: “She was one of the kind that likes to grow up… In the end she grew up of her own free will a day quicker than other girls… she tried for his sake not to have growing pains… she felt she was untrue to him when she got a prize for general knowledge.”

facts.text: Now fully grown-up, Wendy accepts that Peter forgot her, saying it with a smile, and reflects that grown-ups forget how to fly.
facts.argument: "But, alas, he forgot all about me," Wendy said it with a smile... "Because I am grown up... When people grow up they forget the way."

facts.text: She sometimes doubts whether she truly flew as a girl and spends evenings darning by the fire after Jane sleeps.
facts.argument: "Do you know, Jane, I sometimes wonder whether I ever did really fly."; "Wendy was sitting on the floor, very close to the fire, so as to see to darn."

facts.text: One spring night, after finishing the story and while darning by firelight, she hears a crow in the dark nursery.
facts.argument: "It was the spring of the year... and while she sat darning she heard a crow."

facts.text: Wendy is now an adult—"ever so much more than twenty"—a married woman and the mother of Jane; she has forgotten how to fly.
facts.argument: “I am ever so much more than twenty… I am a married woman… the little girl in the bed is my baby… I have forgotten how to fly.”

facts.text: Can no longer fly and, though forlorn, lets Jane fly away with Peter; years pass and she grows old with white hair, last seen watching them fade 'as small as stars.'
facts.argument: "If only I could go with you," Wendy sighed. "You see you can't fly," said Jane; Wendy watches them "until they were as small as stars"; "her hair becoming white... for all this happened long ago."

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Identified as Wendy’s mother; described extensively (romantic mind, sweet mocking mouth, a hidden kiss).

facts.text: Prejudiced in Wendy's favour; loves to have everything just so; supports George's plan to try the budget for a year.
facts.argument: "she was prejudiced in Wendy's favour"; "Mrs. Darling loved to have everything just so"; "Of course we can, George," she cried

facts.text: Nightly, after the children sleep, she "tidies" their minds—repacking thoughts, lingering over discoveries, and setting pretty thoughts on top for morning.
facts.argument: "It is the nightly custom of every good mother... to rummage in their minds and put things straight... When you wake in the morning... on the top... are spread out your prettier thoughts."

facts.text: Once believed in Peter Pan but now, 'married and full of sense,' doubts his existence; after Wendy’s remarks she investigates and finds unfamiliar skeleton leaves near the nursery window, puzzling her.
facts.argument: 'She had believed in him at the time, but… now… doubted'; leaves 'very near the window' and 'did not come from any tree that grew in England.'

facts.text: Fell asleep by the nursery fire during Nana's evening off and awoke to find Peter Pan and a darting light; recognized the boy as Peter Pan.
facts.argument: "She was asleep... while she was dreaming the window... blew open, and a boy did drop on the floor... she knew at once that he was Peter Pan."

facts.text: She rolled up a shadow that had been hanging at the window and put it carefully away in a drawer, intending to show it to Mr. Darling later.
facts.argument: "She decided to roll the shadow up and put it away in a drawer, until a fitting opportunity came for telling her husband."

facts.text: She accepted an invitation to dine at No. 27 on the 'fatal Friday' and later blamed herself for it.
facts.argument: "If only I had not accepted that invitation to dine at 27," Mrs. Darling said.

facts.text: She admits a liking for parties and later blamed this as a factor in the 'fatal Friday' events.
facts.argument: "My liking for parties, George."

facts.text: Remained placid during Mr. Darling’s tie tantrum and 'with her nice cool hands' tied it easily while they were dressing to go out.
facts.argument: "Even then Mrs. Darling was placid… with her nice cool hands she tied his tie for him."

facts.text: Now recalls that evening as 'How wildly we romped!' and regards it as their last romp before events changed the nursery.
facts.argument: "How wildly we romped!" says Mrs. Darling… "Our last romp!" Mr. Darling groaned.

facts.text: She seized the chance to tell her husband about the boy and showed him Peter's shadow.
facts.argument: "It was an opportunity... for telling him about the boy... she showed him the shadow."

facts.text: She and her husband lament that the children are gone.
facts.argument: "They were ours, ours! and now they are gone."

facts.text: She discovered Nana had been given George's medicine, comforted the boys, and tried to hush George so the 'servants' (Liza) would not hear.
facts.argument: She "smelt the bowl" and said, "it's your medicine!"; she "comforted her boys"; "not so loud; the servants will hear you."

facts.text: Before leaving for a party at No. 27, she lit the children's night-lights—"the eyes a mother leaves behind"—sang over them, and, perturbed by a nameless fear about "that boy," wished she weren’t going out.
facts.argument: "Oh, how I wish that I wasn't going to a party to-night!"; she lit their night-lights and called them a mother's eyes; No. 27 was only a few yards distant.

facts.text: Before leaving, she checked the nursery window and found it securely fastened.
facts.argument: "She went to the window. It was securely fastened."

facts.text: With Mr. Darling, she saw four flying shadows on the nursery curtain and tried to reach the nursery quietly, but arrived too late.
facts.argument: She signed Mr. Darling to go softly; they saw "three little figures... Not three figures, four!" yet "rushed into the nursery too late."

facts.text: Selflessly prioritizes her children’s welfare over her own feelings; she would urge observers to focus on the children rather than her sorrow.
facts.argument: “we may be sure that Mrs. Darling does not blame us… she would probably have cried, ‘Don’t be silly; what do I matter? Do go back and keep an eye on the children.’”

facts.text: Awaiting the children's return, she has everything prepared: the beds are aired, she never leaves the house, and the nursery window is kept open.
facts.argument: "All the beds are aired, and she never leaves the house, and observe, the window is open."

facts.text: Grief-stricken and physically worn, she keeps vigil in the night-nursery, dreams her children have returned, and wakes calling their names.
facts.argument: “a very sad-eyed woman… Look at her in her chair… The corner of her mouth… almost withered… her hand moves restlessly… ‘O Nana, I dreamt my dear ones had come back.’”

facts.text: Insists the nursery window be left open at all times for her children's return, refusing to shut it.
facts.argument: "O George, never ask me to do that. The window must always be left open for them, always, always."

facts.text: Plays "Home, Sweet Home" on the nursery piano and weeps while waiting for her children.
facts.argument: She "played" on the nursery piano; Peter sees "two tears ... sitting on her eyes."

facts.text: Upon seeing her children in their beds, she mistakes it for a lingering dream, having so often dreamt of them there.
facts.argument: "She saw them, but she did not believe they were there... she saw them in their beds so often in her dreams that she thought this was just the dream hanging around her still."

facts.text: Immediately agrees to 'have' the six Lost Boys when they present themselves, welcoming them into the household.
facts.argument: "Of course Mrs. Darling said at once that she would have them."

facts.text: Adopts the Lost Boys, offers to adopt Peter (he refuses), and—while keeping Wendy home—allows her a one-week annual visit to Peter for spring cleaning.
facts.argument: "She had adopted all the other boys, and would like to adopt him also." / "Certainly not..." then "made this handsome offer: to let Wendy go to him for a week every year..."

facts.text: Believes (or thought) the fairies were all dead until corrected by Wendy.
facts.argument: Mrs. Darling said, "I thought all the fairies were dead."

facts.text: Her once-reserved kiss was taken by Peter Pan, and she appeared content afterward.
facts.argument: "He took Mrs. Darling's kiss with him... The kiss that had been for no one else... she seemed satisfied."

facts.text: Mrs. Darling has died (“now dead and forgotten”).
facts.argument: “Mrs. Darling was now dead and forgotten.”

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Identified as Wendy’s father; wooed and married Mrs. Darling; prides himself on knowing stocks and shares; careful about household expenses.

facts.text: Meticulously tallies household finances and prospective illness costs (mumps, measles, whooping-cough) to decide if they can "try it for a year" and keep the children; has a passion for being exactly like his neighbours; warns "Remember mumps."
facts.argument: "can we try it for a year on nine nine seven?"; lists mumps, measles, whooping-cough; "Mr. Darling had a passion for being exactly like his neighbours"; "Remember mumps," he warned

facts.text: renamed to 'George Darling'
facts.argument: "Of course we can, George," she cried.

facts.text: Family finances are tight; they are described as poor owing to how much milk the children drank.
facts.argument: "As they were poor, owing to the amount of milk the children drank"

facts.text: Sometimes feels that Nana does not admire him, adding to his anxiety about neighbours' opinions and his position in the city.
facts.argument: "He had sometimes a feeling that she did not admire him... he sometimes wondered uneasily whether the neighbours talked. He had his position in the city to consider."

facts.text: Dismisses talk of Peter Pan as 'nonsense' put into the children’s heads by Nana and expects it to blow over.
facts.argument: "Mark my words… it is some nonsense Nana has been putting into their heads… Leave it alone, and it will blow over."

facts.text: He had a classical education and repeatedly declared himself responsible for what happened that Friday.
facts.argument: "I, George Darling, did it. MEA CULPA, MEA CULPA." He had had a classical education.

facts.text: He sometimes wraps a wet towel around his head to keep his brain clear while doing household calculations.
facts.argument: "with a wet towel around his head to keep his brain clear" while totting up winter great-coats for John and Michael.

facts.text: He later blamed his 'fatal gift of humour' as contributing to the misfortune.
facts.argument: "My fatal gift of humour, dearest."

facts.text: On the evening he and Mrs. Darling dressed for a party, he had a melodramatic outburst over an untied tie—'really yelled' threats about dinner, work, and the children—but accepted her help and soon was playfully dancing with Michael.
facts.argument: "This tie, it will not tie" … "unless this tie is round my neck we don't go out to dinner… I never go to the office again… our children will be flung into the streets" … then "dancing round the room with Michael on his back."

facts.text: Has no real mastery of tying his necktie; sometimes manages it on a bedpost and even considers a made-up tie.
facts.argument: "though he knew about stocks and shares, had no real mastery of his tie" … "twenty times have I made it up round the bed-post" … "used a made-up tie."

facts.text: Remembers the evening as their 'last romp' with the children, groaning about it in retrospect.
facts.argument: "Our last romp!" Mr. Darling groaned.

facts.text: He examined Peter Pan's shadow; though he initially pooh-poohed the story, seeing the shadow made him thoughtful, and he judged it looked a 'scoundrel.'
facts.argument: "At first he pooh-poohed the story, but he became thoughtful when she showed him the shadow... 'it does look a scoundrel.'"

facts.text: Despite boasting he took medicine bravely as a child, he had secretly hidden his own 'nastier' medicine bottle atop the wardrobe.
facts.argument: He claimed he'd take his medicine as an example "if I hadn't lost the bottle"—but had climbed to the top of the wardrobe and hidden it there.

facts.text: He was distressed when Nana's hair soiled his first-ever braided new trousers, biting his lip to hold back tears.
facts.argument: He "collided against her, covering his trousers with hairs... first he had ever had with braid... had to bite his lip to prevent the tears coming."

facts.text: He mourns with his wife that their children are gone.
facts.argument: "They were ours, ours! and now they are gone."

facts.text: Dodged taking his medicine by pretending to comply, then poured his dose into Nana's bowl; afterward felt ashamed yet stayed defensive, complaining that nobody coddles him though he is the breadwinner.
facts.argument: "slipped his [medicine] behind his back"; "I shall pour my medicine into Nana's bowl"; "Mr. Darling was frightfully ashamed of himself"; "Nobody coddles me... I am only the breadwinner"

facts.text: In a bid to assert authority, he forced Nana out of the nursery and tied her up in the back-yard, then sat ashamed, his vanity craving admiration despite remorse.
facts.argument: "the proper place for you is the yard..."; "seizing her roughly, dragged her"; "He was ashamed of himself... craved for admiration."

facts.text: He and Mrs. Darling saw four flying shadows on the nursery curtain and rushed upstairs but arrived too late to stop the children leaving.
facts.argument: They saw "three little figures... Not three figures, four!" and "Mr. and Mrs. Darling... rushed into the nursery too late."

facts.text: In anger he chained Nana in the yard, which preceded the children flying away.
facts.argument: "Mr. Darling was angry with her and chained her up in the yard, and so all the children flew away."

facts.text: In deep remorse for chaining Nana and acknowledging she was wiser, he crawled into her kennel and swore not to leave it until the children return; he acts in excess when he commits to something.
facts.argument: "All the blame was his for having chained Nana up, and that from first to last she had been wiser than he... he went down on all fours and crawled into the kennel... he swore that he would never leave the kennel until his children came back... whatever Mr. Darling did he had to do in excess."

facts.text: Despite his simplicity and boyish air (baldness aside), he possesses a noble sense of justice and a lion’s courage to do what seems right to him.
facts.argument: "He was quite a simple man... indeed he might have passed for a boy again if he had been able to take his baldness off; but he had also a noble sense of justice and a lion's courage to do what seemed right to him."

facts.text: Humbles himself by living and even commuting in Nana’s kennel; defers to Nana’s wishes; maintains calm courtesy despite public scrutiny and becomes a minor celebrity (crowds, autographs, interviews, society invites him to dinner “in the kennel”).
facts.argument: “sat in the kennel… every morning the kennel was carried… crowd… girls scaled it to get his autograph… interviews… ‘Do come in the kennel.’… ‘he always lifted his hat courteously’… ‘followed her wishes implicitly.’

facts.text: Appears more worn than before but with a softer expression as he continues his public penance.
facts.argument: “his face is more worn than of yore, but has a softer expression.”

facts.text: Is living in Nana’s kennel as a self-imposed punishment and remains full of remorse, even curling up to sleep there.
facts.argument: "See my punishment: living in a kennel" ... then, feeling drowsy, he curled round in the kennel.

facts.text: Receives social attention for his kennel penance but remains modest and kinder, not letting success spoil him.
facts.argument: "There were several adults to-day"; "Social success had not spoilt him; it had made him sweeter."

facts.text: He is sleeping inside Nana's kennel in the nursery.
facts.argument: "'The kennel!' ... 'there's a man inside it.' ... 'It's father!'"

facts.text: Initially feels slighted for not being consulted about taking in the Lost Boys and behaves unworthily, calling himself treated as a 'cypher,' then bursts into tears and cheerfully commits to finding space for all of them, leading them with 'Follow the leader... Hoop la!'
facts.argument: He 'thought they should have asked his consent... instead of treating him as a cypher'; then he 'burst into tears' and said he'd 'find space for them all' and cried 'Follow the leader... Hoop la!'

facts.text: In old age he became “no longer fond of stairs” and sold the nursery to his son-in-law (Jane’s father). He is now a widower after Mrs. Darling’s death.
facts.argument: “It was Jane’s nursery now, for her father had bought it… from Wendy’s father, who was no longer fond of stairs. Mrs. Darling was now dead…”

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Mentioned as the second child: "Wendy came first, then John, then Michael."

facts.text: Attends Miss Fulsom's Kindergarten; has 'footer' (football) days at school.
facts.argument: "the three of them going in a row to Miss Fulsom's Kindergarten"; "On John's footer days she never once forgot his sweater"

facts.text: In his imagined Neverland, John lived in a boat turned upside down on the sands, had a lagoon with flamingoes he was shooting, and had no friends there.
facts.argument: "John's ... had a lagoon with flamingoes ... at which John was shooting ... John lived in a boat turned upside down ... John had no friends."

facts.text: Play-acted as his father at Wendy’s birth, gave 'extra pomp' to his own, and told Michael 'they did not want any more,' making Michael nearly cry.
facts.argument: "I am happy to inform you, Mrs. Darling, that you are now a mother" … "with the extra pomp" … "John said brutally that they did not want any more."

facts.text: He cheerily reassured his father about taking the medicine, saying it would soon be over.
facts.argument: "It will soon be over, father," John said cheerily.

facts.text: Upset by Nana being chained, he whimpered that her barking was because she was being tied in the yard.
facts.argument: "John whimpered, 'It is because he is chaining her up in the yard.'"

facts.text: Briefly takes command in the nursery, ordering lights out and hiding upon sensing danger; the narrator notes this is his only command during the adventure.
facts.argument: "Out with the light! Hide! Quick!" cried John, taking command for the only time throughout the whole adventure.

facts.text: A practical boy who asked Peter to demonstrate slowly; experienced his first flight after receiving fairy dust.
facts.argument: "He was quite a practical boy... 'couldn't you do it very slowly once?'"; after Peter blew fairy dust, "John let go" and flew.

facts.text: Eager for adventure—upon hearing there are pirates, he grabbed his Sunday hat and wanted to leave at once.
facts.argument: "'Pirates,' cried John, seizing his Sunday hat, 'let us go at once.'"

facts.text: Can now fly strongly but remains somewhat clumsy, tending to kick too much and bump into clouds when trying to avoid them.
facts.argument: "They could now fly strongly... the more they tried to avoid [a cloud], the more certainly did they bump into it."

facts.text: Claims he can read smoke to judge if the natives are on the war-path; comparatively brave yet cautious about adventures.
facts.argument: “I’ll tell you by the way smoke curls whether they are on the war-path.” / “the braver John hesitated… ‘What kind of adventure?’”

facts.text: Aghast at serving Wendy and at building her a house, exclaiming "she is only a girl," and initially considering waking her to make supper.
facts.argument: John: "Build a house?" … "For Wendy? … Why, she is only a girl!" Earlier, he watches as Michael proposes waking her to make supper.

facts.text: John needed slight alteration by Peter to fit his hollow tree; after a few days’ practice he could go up and down with the breath-control technique.
facts.argument: "John had to be altered a little." / "After a few days' practice they could go up and down... by drawing in and letting out alternately."

facts.text: John’s memory of his parents has faded; he now recalls them only vaguely as people he once knew and struggled to answer Wendy’s exam questions, making many crosses.
facts.argument: “John remembered his parents vaguely only, as people he had once known… it was really dreadful what a number of crosses even John made.”

facts.text: Introduced a new method in the mermaids' bubble game by heading the bubble; described as the one mark he has left on Neverland.
facts.argument: “John introduced a new way of hitting the bubble, with the head… This is the one mark that John has left on the Neverland.”

facts.text: Showed combat bravery at the lagoon, being first to draw blood; he boarded the boat, grappled with Starkey, and leapt overboard after him.
facts.argument: “First to draw blood was John, who gallantly climbed into the boat and held Starkey … He wriggled overboard and John leapt after him.”

facts.text: Challenges Peter’s father role, asking to sit in Peter’s chair and asserting Peter "is not really our father," claiming he taught Peter how a father behaves.
facts.argument: "May I sit in Peter's chair..."; "He is not really our father... He didn't even know how a father does till I showed him."

facts.text: He teasingly claimed to know Mr. and Mrs. Darling during Wendy's story to annoy the others.
facts.argument: "'I knew them,' John said, to annoy the others."

facts.text: Joins Michael in urging to go home and decides to leave Neverland with Wendy.
facts.argument: "'Wendy, let us [let's] go home,' cried John and Michael together."

facts.text: Patriotically refused Hook's offer to become a pirate when told he must swear 'Down with the King,' striking the barrel; had once thought of the pirate alias 'Red-handed Jack.'
facts.argument: "Shall we still be respectful subjects of the King?" ... Hook: "You would have to swear, 'Down with the King.'" John: "Then I refuse," banging the barrel; earlier: "I once thought of calling myself Red-handed Jack."

facts.text: Serves as second mate under Captain Pan aboard the Jolly Roger.
facts.argument: “Nibs and John were first and second mate.”

facts.text: He is on the return voyage to the mainland/home aboard the Jolly Roger, serving as second mate.
facts.argument: “Nibs and John were first and second mate… turned the ship… for the mainland… lawful occupants are on their way home.”

facts.text: He, with Wendy and Michael, is planning a surprise return home from the ship, expecting to arrive 'Thursday week' and delight their parents.
facts.argument: "They have been planning it out on the ship... the children are coming back... they will be here on Thursday week."

facts.text: Currently flying home to the Darling house; within two miles of the window.
facts.argument: “They are really within two miles of the window now, and flying strong.”

facts.text: Shows fading memory of home, uncertain whether his father used to sleep in the kennel.
facts.argument: "'Surely,' said John... 'he used not to sleep in the kennel?'"

facts.text: Returns home and reunites with his parents during the emotional nursery scene.
facts.argument: "That's John," she said... they went round Wendy and John and Michael; Mr. Darling woke to share her bliss.

facts.text: After returning and starting school, he gradually lost the power to fly as his belief faded and settled into ordinary life.
facts.argument: "Soon they settled down to being as ordinary... It is sad... the power to fly gradually left them... what it really meant was that they no longer believed."

facts.text: John grew up into a bearded man with children of his own but doesn’t know any stories to tell them.
facts.argument: “The bearded man who doesn't know any story to tell his children was once John.”

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "There was the same excitement over John, and Michael had even a narrower squeak; but both were kept, and soon, you might have seen the three of them going in a row to Miss Fulsom's Kindergarten school"

facts.text: Attends Miss Fulsom's Kindergarten with his siblings.
facts.argument: "the three of them going in a row to Miss Fulsom's Kindergarten school"

facts.text: In his imagined Neverland, Michael (being very small) had a flamingo with lagoons flying over it, lived in a wigwam, and had friends at night.
facts.argument: "Michael, who was very small, had a flamingo with lagoons flying over it. ... Michael in a wigwam ... Michael had friends at night."

facts.text: Sensitive about being wanted; asked to be 'born' too, said 'Nobody wants me,' then leapt into his mother’s arms when reassured; later romped on his father’s back.
facts.argument: "Michael came from his bath to ask to be born also" … "Nobody wants me" … "Then he had leapt into her arms" … "dancing round the room with Michael on his back."

facts.text: He refused to take his medicine, dodging Nana's spoon and crying, "Won't; won't!"
facts.argument: "Michael dodged the spoon in Nana's mouth... 'Won't; won't!'"

facts.text: He once asked his mother, "How did you get to know me, mother?" suggesting childlike curiosity.
facts.argument: "Michael suddenly said to me, 'How did you get to know me, mother?'"

facts.text: Shown to be of a suspicious nature; he took his medicine promptly and angrily called his father a "cowardly custard" when Mr. Darling dodged his dose.
facts.argument: "who was of a suspicious nature"; Wendy counted and "Michael took his medicine"; he yelled and said, "Father's a cowardly custard."

facts.text: Concerned about safety, he asked his mother if anything could harm them after the night-lights were lit; she reassured him.
facts.argument: "Can anything harm us, mother, after the night-lights are lit?" "Nothing, precious," she said.

facts.text: Gallantly let go first and achieved his first flight, exclaiming "I flewed!"
facts.argument: "gallant Michael let go first... immediately he was borne across the room. 'I flewed!' he screamed."

facts.text: Displays eager, naive curiosity about distance and speed; wanted to see how long a billion miles would take and raced John, getting a start.
facts.argument: "Michael was ready: he wanted to see how long it took him to do a billion miles... John and Michael raced, Michael getting a start."

facts.text: Can now fly strongly but remains somewhat clumsy, tending to kick too much and bump into clouds when trying to avoid them.
facts.argument: "They could now fly strongly... the more they tried to avoid [a cloud], the more certainly did they bump into it."

facts.text: Relieved when Wendy chooses tea before adventure; he presses her hand in gratitude.
facts.argument: “Wendy said ‘tea first’ quickly, and Michael pressed her hand in gratitude.”

facts.text: Fitted his hollow tree on the first try and soon mastered the breath-control technique to go up and down; he also grew to love the underground home.
facts.argument: "Wendy and Michael fitted their trees at the first try." / "After a few days' practice they could go up and down..." / "And how ardently they grew to love their home under the ground; especially Wendy."

facts.text: Slept hung in a basket as the household’s “baby,” rather than sharing the boys’ bed.
facts.argument: “all the boys slept in it, except Michael… Wendy… desired a baby… he was hung up in a basket.”

facts.text: Michael had made a kite days earlier that once lifted him off the ground; it tore free and later its tail reached Peter, enabling Wendy's escape.
facts.argument: "It was the tail of a kite, which Michael had made some days before... It lifted Michael off the ground..."

facts.text: Michael and Curly once attempted to have his kite lift two people at once, but it failed.
facts.argument: "It can't lift two; Michael and Curly tried."

facts.text: Despite protesting he is too big, he is placed in a cradle/basket as the 'littlest.'
facts.argument: "I'm too big for a cradle"; "He was already in his basket."

facts.text: He claims credit for teaching Peter to call mothers 'old lady.'
facts.argument: Michael whispered to Curly: "It was me told him mothers are called old lady."

facts.text: Joins John in urging to go home and decides to leave Neverland with Wendy.
facts.argument: "'Wendy, let us [let's] go home,' cried John and Michael together."

facts.text: Despite being impressed by the offered pirate name 'Blackbeard Joe,' he refused to join Hook after learning he must renounce the King.
facts.argument: Hook: "Blackbeard Joe." ... "Then I refuse," cried Michael.

facts.text: Killed a pirate during the battle and proudly showed Wendy where it happened.
facts.argument: "Michael showed her the place where he had killed one."

facts.text: During the return voyage on the captured Jolly Roger, he served as a common sailor (“tar”) living in the fo’c’sle and donned pirate clothes.
facts.argument: “They all donned pirate clothes… The rest were tars before the mast, and lived in the fo’c’sle.”

facts.text: He, with Wendy and John, is planning a surprise return home from the ship, expecting to arrive 'Thursday week' and delight their parents.
facts.argument: "They have been planning it out on the ship... the children are coming back... they will be here on Thursday week."

facts.text: Currently flying home to the Darling house; within two miles of the window.
facts.argument: “They are really within two miles of the window now, and flying strong.”

facts.text: Momentarily forgets his home upon return, doubting his familiarity with the nursery.
facts.argument: "the youngest one had already forgotten his home... 'I think I have been here before.'"

facts.text: Boasts that he killed a pirate, comparing his father's size unfavorably to that pirate.
facts.argument: "He is not so big as the pirate I killed," Michael said.

facts.text: Returns home and reunites with his parents, joining the embrace with Wendy and John.
facts.argument: "Mother!" cried Michael... they went round Wendy and John and Michael; Mr. Darling woke to share her bliss.

facts.text: Maintained belief in flying longer than the other boys and was present when Peter came for Wendy at the end of the first year.
facts.argument: "Michael believed longer than the other boys... so he was with Wendy when Peter came for her at the end of the first year."

facts.text: Michael became an engine-driver (train engineer).
facts.argument: “Michael is an engine-driver [train engineer].”

summaries.text: Michael Darling is the youngest child of the Darling family, brother to Wendy and John. He attends Miss Fulsom's Kindergarten with his siblings.

Michael Darling is the youngest of the Darling siblings, brother to Wendy and John, and a student at Miss Fulsom's Kindergarten. Sensitive and imaginative, he craves reassurance and displays curiosity, often expressing concern for safety and showing a playful spirit.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "this nurse was a prim Newfoundland dog, called Nana, who had belonged to no one in particular until the Darlings engaged her"

facts.text: A prim Newfoundland dog hired by the Darlings as a nurse due to tight finances; met them in Kensington Gardens where she peeped into perambulators and reported careless nursemaids. Thorough at bath-time, up at night if a child cries; kennel in the nursery; judges which coughs need attention; favors old remedies like rhubarb leaf and scorns new talk of germs; escorts the children to school, keeps them in line, remembers John's sweater on footer days, and carries an umbrella in her mouth.
facts.argument: "this nurse was a prim Newfoundland dog, called Nana"; "the Darlings had become acquainted with her in Kensington Gardens... peeping into perambulators"; "complained of [careless nursemaids] to their mistresses"; details on bath-time, night, kennel, coughs, remedies; "escort[ing] the children to school"; "On John's footer days she never once forgot his sweater"; "she usually carried an umbrella in her mouth"

facts.text: Among the human nurses at Miss Fulsom's school she is treated as socially inferior and she despises their light talk; she resents visits from Mrs. Darling's friends but meticulously grooms the children for them.
facts.argument: "They affected to ignore her as of an inferior social status... and she despised their light talk." / "She resented visits... but... whipped off Michael's pinafore... smoothed out Wendy and made a dash at John's hair."

facts.text: Her management of the nursery is impeccably correct, as even Mr. Darling acknowledges.
facts.argument: "No nursery could possibly have been conducted more correctly, and Mr. Darling knew it."

facts.text: Returned from her evening out when Mrs. Darling screamed; attempted to attack Peter Pan, then captured his shadow by slamming the window.
facts.argument: "as if in answer to a bell... Nana entered... sprang at the boy... As he leapt at the window Nana had closed it quickly... slam went the window and snapped it off."

facts.text: Hung Peter Pan's detached shadow out the nursery window so he could retrieve it without waking the children.
facts.argument: "Nana... hung it out at the window, meaning 'He is sure to come back for it; let us put it where he can get it easily without disturbing the children.'"

facts.text: She considers herself touchy about trifles.
facts.argument: "My touchiness about trifles, dear master and mistress."

facts.text: She later wished she had pretended to like the medicine after Mr. Darling poured his dose into her bowl.
facts.argument: "If only I had pretended to like the medicine," was what Nana's wet eyes said.

facts.text: Shares in the family’s recollections of the evening when Michael feared being unwanted, remembered as possibly his last night in the nursery.
facts.argument: "Such a little thing for Mr. and Mrs. Darling and Nana to recall now, but not so little if that was to be Michael's last night in the nursery."

facts.text: She brought Michael's medicine carrying the bottle in her mouth; Mr. Darling declared she would never do that again and took the blame.
facts.argument: "Nana came in with Michael's medicine... 'You will never carry the bottle in your mouth again, Nana, and it is all my fault.'"

facts.text: After being made to drink Mr. Darling's medicine, she displayed wounded dignity—showing a 'great red tear'—and withdrew to her kennel.
facts.argument: She "began lapping it"; then "showed him the great red tear" and "crept into her kennel."

facts.text: Removed from the nursery and chained in the back-yard; barked her danger-bark while separated from the children.
facts.argument: "tied her up in the back-yard"; Wendy: "That is not Nana's unhappy bark... that is her bark when she smells danger."

facts.text: Has a kennel in the nursery; she had to be lured out before being tied in the back-yard.
facts.argument: "commands would not draw Nana from the kennel, he lured her out of it... tied her up in the back-yard."

facts.text: Had been barking distressfully all evening; her sudden silence alarms the children.
facts.argument: "Nana, who had been barking distressfully all the evening, was quiet now. It was her silence they had heard."

facts.text: Broke her chain and burst into the Darlings’ dining-room, signaling an emergency by flinging up her paws to heaven.
facts.argument: "she broke it... burst into the dining-room of 27 and flung up her paws to heaven," her way of making a communication.

facts.text: Accompanied the Darlings in rushing back into the nursery, but was too late to prevent the children's departure.
facts.argument: "Mr. and Mrs. Darling and Nana rushed into the nursery too late. The birds were flown."

facts.text: She was chained in the yard by Mr. Darling despite being a faithful nurse.
facts.argument: "a faithful nurse called Nana; but Mr. Darling was angry with her and chained her up in the yard"

facts.text: Rushes into the nursery during the family's emotional reunion after the children's return.
facts.argument: "Nana came rushing in."

facts.text: Initially tied the boys' feet to the bed-posts at night to prevent them from flying away.
facts.argument: "At first Nana tied their feet to the bed-posts so that they should not fly away in the night."

facts.text: Nana died of old age; toward the end she was difficult and firmly believed no one but herself knew how to look after children.
facts.argument: “there was no kennel, for Nana also had passed away. She died of old age, and at the end she had been rather difficult… very firmly convinced that no one knew how to look after children except herself.”

summaries.text: Nana, the Darlings' devoted Newfoundland dog nurse, is a practical caregiver known for her thoroughness and old-fashioned remedies. She ensures the children's well-being, escorts them to school, and is always prepared, even carrying an umbrella in her mouth.

Nana, the Darlings' Newfoundland dog nurse, is a diligent caregiver known for her old-fashioned remedies and thoroughness. She manages the nursery, escorts the children to school, and carries an umbrella in her mouth, while resenting the social dynamics with human nurses.
