facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "Miss Fulsom's Kindergarten school"

facts.text: Her school's basement includes a waiting room where nurses wait on forms; Nana lies on the floor there.
facts.argument: "There is a room in the basement of Miss Fulsom's school where the nurses wait. They sat on forms, while Nana lay on the floor."

summaries.text: Kindergarten schoolmistress whose school Wendy, John, and Michael attend.

Miss Fulsom is the kindergarten schoolmistress at the school attended by Wendy, John, and Michael. Her school's basement features a waiting room for nurses, where Nana is often found lying on the floor.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "The only other servant, Liza, was sometimes allowed to join" the family dances.

facts.text: A diminutive maid who sometimes joins the family romps; looked tiny in her long skirt and maid's cap and claimed, when hired, that she would "never see ten again."
facts.argument: "Such a midget she looked in her long skirt and maid's cap, though she had sworn, when engaged, that she would never see ten again."

facts.text: She discovered the medicine bottle Mr. Darling hid on top of the wardrobe and returned it to his wash-stand.
facts.argument: "The faithful Liza had found it, and put it back on his wash-stand."

facts.text: Described as faithful; she discreetly corrected Mr. Darling's hidden-medicine ruse by returning the bottle to his wash-stand.
facts.argument: "the faithful Liza had found it, and put it back on his wash-stand."

facts.text: In the household she is collectively referred to as "the servants," implying she is their only servant.
facts.argument: "Somehow they had got into the way of calling Liza the servants."

facts.text: Sternly restrained Nana despite her alarm, tying her up and threatening to fetch the Darlings if Nana barked again.
facts.argument: "No more of it, Nana," she said sternly... "if you bark again I shall go straight for master and missus... won't master whip you"... She tied the unhappy dog up again.

facts.text: Scornful of Mr. Darling’s kennel penance; lacks imagination and sneers that the cheering crowd are merely little boys.
facts.argument: “she took it scornfully; for she had no imagination… ‘Lots of little boys,’ sneered Liza.”

summaries.text: Liza is a small-statured maid serving the Darlings, often joining their adventures. She humorously claims she will 'never see ten again,' emphasizing her diminutive size, especially in her long skirt and maid's cap.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "There never was a simpler happier family until the coming of Peter Pan. Mrs. Darling first heard of Peter..."

facts.text: His arrival marks a turning point for the Darling family, who were a simpler, happier household until his coming.
facts.argument: "There never was a simpler happier family until the coming of Peter Pan."

facts.text: Mrs. Darling recalls from childhood that Peter Pan was said to live with the fairies and to accompany children part of the way when they died so they would not be frightened.
facts.argument: "she just remembered a Peter Pan who was said to live with the fairies ... when children died he went part of the way with them"

facts.text: Allegedly visits the Darlings’ nursery at night via the window, sits on Wendy’s bed, and plays his pipes; leaves near the window suggest his presence; he remains child-sized like Wendy.
facts.argument: Wendy: 'I think he comes in by the window' … 'sat on the foot of her bed and played on his pipes'; leaves found very near the window; 'he isn't grown up… just my size.'

facts.text: Dropped into the Darling nursery at night through the open window, accompanied by a small, darting light.
facts.argument: "the window of the nursery blew open, and a boy did drop on the floor... He was accompanied by a strange light, no bigger than your fist"

facts.text: His detached shadow remained in the Darlings' nursery and was later shown to Mr. Darling, who examined it and disparaged it as a 'scoundrel.'
facts.argument: "she showed him the shadow"; Mr. Darling: "It is nobody I know... but it does look a scoundrel."

facts.text: Has a mischievous habit of trying to blow out stars; despite their usual displeasure, the stars are on his side tonight to get the grown-ups away.
facts.argument: "Peter... had a mischievous way of ... trying to blow them out"; "they were on his side to-night, and anxious to get the grown-ups out of the way."

facts.text: Peter arrives in the Darling nursery with Tinker Bell, searching for his lost shadow, and unsuccessfully tries to reattach it with soap before crying.
facts.argument: "Peter dropped in... looking for Peter's shadow... tried to stick it on with soap... sat on the floor and cried."

facts.text: Gives his address as "Second to the right and then straight on till morning" and says he doesn't receive letters.
facts.argument: “Second to the right … and then straight on till morning.” / “Don’t get any letters,” he said contemptuously.

facts.text: Says he has no mother and does not want one, thinking mothers are overrated.
facts.argument: “Don’t have a mother,” … “Not only had he no mother, but he had not the slightest desire to have one. He thought them very over-rated persons.”

facts.text: Had lost his shadow, tried to stick it on with soap, and after it was sewn on believed he had done it himself.
facts.argument: Shadow lay on the floor; he had been trying to stick it on with soap; later “He thought he had attached the shadow himself.”

facts.text: Exceptionally conceited and boastful, crowing “How clever I am!”, and insists he never cries.
facts.argument: “there never was a cockier boy”; “oh, the cleverness of me!”; “he was already of the opinion that he had never cried in his life.”

facts.text: Shows ignorance of sewing; asks “What’s sewn?” when Wendy proposes sewing his shadow.
facts.argument: “‘It must be sewn on,’ … ‘What’s sewn?’ he asked.”

facts.text: Is indifferent to appearances, even when Wendy suggests ironing his shadow.
facts.argument: “Peter, boylike, was indifferent to appearances,” after Wendy says, “Perhaps I should have ironed it.”

facts.text: Says he doesn’t know his age; claims he “ran away the day I was born” after hearing his parents discuss what he’d be when a man. Declares he never wants to grow up, wants always to be a little boy and have fun, and says he ran to Kensington Gardens and lived a long time among the fairies (he knows fairies).
facts.argument: “I don’t know… I ran away the day I was born… I don’t want ever to be a man… So I ran away to Kensington Gardens and lived a long long time among the fairies.”

facts.text: He recounts fairy lore: says fairies began when the first baby's laugh broke into pieces; claims there ought to be one fairy per child but many die when children say they don't believe.
facts.argument: "when the first baby laughed... that was the beginning of fairies"; "there ought to be one fairy for every boy and girl"; "every time a child says, 'I don't believe in fairies,' there is a fairy... that falls down dead."

facts.text: Peter Pan lives mostly with the Lost Boys in Neverland and is their captain; he lacks knowledge of stories and confuses kisses with thimbles.
facts.argument: "With the lost boys." "I'm captain." and "I don't know any stories"; he offers a thimble for a kiss.

facts.text: He offers to teach Wendy (and her brothers) how to fly, describing it as "jump[ing] on the wind's back."
facts.argument: "I'll teach you... I'll teach you how to jump on the wind's back, and then away we go"; "Peter Pan has come and he is to teach us to fly."

facts.text: Displays manipulative cunning to recruit Wendy as a mother for the boys, with a greedy look, sly tactics, and no pity for her reluctance.
facts.argument: "there was a greedy look in his eyes"; "He had become frightfully cunning... the sly one... he had no pity for her."

facts.text: Explains that flying requires thinking lovely thoughts but also needs fairy dust; he blew dust on each child to enable their flight; he also "did not know A from Z," indicating illiteracy.
facts.argument: "You just think lovely wonderful thoughts..."; "no one can fly unless the fairy dust has been blown on him... he blew some on each of them"; and "Peter did not know A from Z."

facts.text: Boastfully declared himself "sweet" and forgot his manners while showing off his flying.
facts.argument: "How sweet!" cried Wendy. "Yes, I'm sweet, oh, I am sweet!" said Peter, forgetting his manners again.

facts.text: Gave Wendy directions to Neverland as "Second to the right, and straight on till morning," but his directions are unreliable—he tends to say whatever comes into his head.
facts.argument: "That, Peter had told Wendy, was the way to the Neverland... Peter, you see, just said anything that came into his head."

facts.text: Peter is recklessly showy in flight, delaying rescues to the last moment and forgetting basic instruction (like how to stop), seeming more interested in his cleverness than safety; he may even let someone fall if bored.
facts.argument: "always waited till the last moment... it was his cleverness that interested him..."; "fond of variety... possibility that the next time you fell he would let you go"; "Peter had forgotten to show them how to stop."

facts.text: Frequently darts ahead for solo adventures mid-flight, returning laughing and sometimes with mermaid scales on him, yet unable to say for certain what happened.
facts.argument: "He would suddenly shoot out of sight... he would come up with mermaid scales still sticking to him, and yet not be able to say for certain what had been happening."

facts.text: His memory is unreliable; he quickly forgets recent adventures and can even forget his companions unless reminded.
facts.argument: "he had already forgotten what it was"; "sometimes when he returned he did not remember them"

facts.text: Leads like a captain and instructs others in flight, teaching them to lie flat on a strong following wind to sleep and calling, "We get off here."
facts.argument: "he showed them how to lie out flat on a strong wind... they could sleep thus"; "soon he would cry in his captain voice, 'We get off here.'"

facts.text: Tires quickly of sleeping during the journey, preferring action and to move on.
facts.argument: "Peter tired quickly of sleeping, and soon he would cry in his captain voice, 'We get off here.'"

facts.text: Drops his careless manner and shows striking courage, even beating the air to force a way; casually proposes killing a sleeping pirate.
facts.argument: “His careless manner had gone… His courage was almost appalling… until Peter had beaten on it with his fists… ‘There’s a pirate asleep… we’ll go down and kill him.’”

facts.text: Briefly annoyed that the children know so much about the island and inclined to ‘lord it over’ them.
facts.argument: “Peter was a little annoyed with them for knowing so much… if he wanted to lord it over them his triumph was at hand.”

facts.text: When asked who the hostile forces are that resist their landing, he cannot or will not say; he scouts by listening intently and peering down with piercing eyes.
facts.argument: “‘They don’t want us to land,’… ‘Who are they?’… But he could not or would not say… listening intently, hand to his ear… eyes so bright.”

facts.text: Hates lethargy; his return energizes Neverland and sets all its factions in motion.
facts.argument: "with the coming of Peter, who hates lethargy, they are under way again"

facts.text: Enforces a rule against the Lost Boys growing up, and 'thins them out' when they seem to be growing up.
facts.argument: "when they seem to be growing up, which is against the rules, Peter thins them out;"

facts.text: Exercises strict control over his band’s knowledge; since he didn’t know what twins were, he did not allow the boys to know either.
facts.argument: "Peter never quite knew what twins were, and his band were not allowed to know anything he did not know,"

facts.text: Forbids talk of mothers among the Lost Boys, calling the subject "silly."
facts.argument: "It was only in Peter's absence that they could speak of mothers, the subject being forbidden by him as silly."

facts.text: He severed Captain Hook's hand and threw it to a crocodile, which gave the beast a taste for Hook and fueled their endless feud.
facts.argument: Hook: "'Twas he cut off my arm... Peter flung my arm... to a crocodile that happened to be passing by."

facts.text: When facing wolves, Peter's known tactic is to look at them through his legs.
facts.argument: "Peter would look at them through his legs."

facts.text: Crows as a signal of his return.
facts.argument: “They heard Peter crow… for it was always thus that he signalled his return.”

facts.text: On seeing Wendy apparently dead, he awkwardly suggested she might be frightened of being dead and considered ‘hopping off’ to avoid the scene, showing evasive, childlike handling of grief.
facts.argument: “She is dead… Perhaps she is frightened at being dead.” He thought of “hopping off in a comic sort of way… and then never going near the spot any more.”

facts.text: Protectively forbids anyone from touching Wendy and orders a little house built around her, measuring her with his feet and specifying chairs and a fender first.
facts.argument: "You must not touch her... Let us build a little house round her." He measured Wendy with his feet; "Chairs and a fender first."

facts.text: To Peter, make-believe and truth are identical; he enforces the pretense, even rapping the boys on the knuckles if they break it.
facts.argument: "to him make-believe and true were exactly the same... If they broke down... he rapped them on the knuckles."

facts.text: Claimed credit for a good idea that was not his (regarding the house).
facts.argument: "Peter, seeing this to be a good idea, at once pretended that it was his own."

facts.text: Acts as vigilant guardian and leader: kept armed watch outside the little house at night with drawn sword against pirates and wolves; also measures—and if needed alters—children to fit their individual hollow tree entrances (did so for Wendy, John, and Michael).
facts.argument: "Peter kept watch outside with drawn sword, for the pirates could be heard... and the wolves were on the prowl." / "One of the first things Peter did next day was to measure Wendy and John and Michael for hollow trees... if... odd shape, Peter does some things to you, and after that you fit."

facts.text: His whim dictates whether meals are real or make‑believe; he only eats when it is part of a game, yet make‑believe is so real to him he seems to grow rounder during it; he permits ‘stodging’ if one proves they’re getting loose for their tree.
facts.argument: “it all depended upon Peter’s whim: he could eat… if it was part of a game… Make‑believe was so real to him… you could see him getting rounder… if you could prove… getting loose for your tree he let you stodge.”

facts.text: Peter despises all mothers except Wendy, and he is the only boy on the island who can neither write nor spell.
facts.argument: “he despised all mothers except Wendy… he was the only boy on the island who could neither write nor spell; not the smallest word.”

facts.text: Peter has a peculiar habit of switching sides mid-fight, treating battles like games.
facts.argument: “showing one of Peter’s peculiarities… in the middle of a fight he would suddenly change sides… ‘I’m redskin to-day’.”

facts.text: Peter invented a game of pretending not to have adventures, briefly enjoying ordinary activities.
facts.argument: “Peter invented… a new game… pretending not to have adventures… sitting on stools… going out for walks.”

facts.text: Peter’s accounts of adventures are unreliable: he sometimes forgets them entirely or boasts without evidence.
facts.argument: “He often went out alone… you were never absolutely certain… he might have forgotten it… and then… you found the body;… or he might say a great deal… and yet you could not find the body.”

facts.text: He quickly loses interest in games once the novelty fades.
facts.argument: “fascinated him enormously, until he suddenly had no more interest in it, which… always happened with his games.”

facts.text: Peter can sense danger even in his sleep and reacts instantly, warning of pirates and ordering the boys to dive.
facts.argument: "one among them who could sniff danger even in his sleep. Peter sprang erect... 'Pirates!'... 'Dive!'"

facts.text: In moments of danger Peter wears a strange smile that asserts his authority, making others silent and ready to obey.
facts.argument: "A strange smile was playing about his face... While that smile was on his face no one dared address him; all they could do was to stand ready to obey."

facts.text: Imitated Hook’s voice to trick the pirates into freeing Tiger Lily, then nearly crowed with pride—showing daring and conceit.
facts.argument: "Ahoy there, you lubbers!" (in Hook’s voice) ... "Set her free"; later, "Am I not a wonder..." and described as "top-heavy with conceit."

facts.text: Forgets past tragedies and acts on a sense of fair play; angered by two-against-one odds, he intervenes despite danger.
facts.argument: "Peter had seen many tragedies, but he had forgotten them all... it was two against one that angered him, and he meant to save her."

facts.text: Adept at voice mimicry and unable to resist games; during a guessing game he proudly revealed, “I am Peter Pan,” then rallied the Lost Boys to attack the pirates and sought Hook as the “bigger game.”
facts.argument: “Have you another voice?” “I have.” … “Well, then,” he cried, “I am Peter Pan.” … “Are you ready, boys?” … “Then lam into the pirates.” … “He was seeking bigger game.”

facts.text: Peter will not fight unfairly and even helps foes up; when treated unfairly he is shocked each time but then forgets it.
facts.argument: "It would not have been fighting fair. He gave the pirate a hand... No one ever gets over the first unfairness; no one except Peter... he always forgot it."

facts.text: On Marooners' Rock he was bitten and clawed by Hook, yet managed to haul fainted Wendy onto the rock before himself fainting as the tide rose (near-drowning).
facts.argument: "Hook bit him... Twice the iron hand clawed him... With a last effort Peter pulled her up the rock... Even as he also fainted he saw that the water was rising."

facts.text: Wounded and unable to fly or swim, Peter faces drowning on Marooners' Rock but regains composure, embracing death as an adventure: "To die will be an awfully big adventure."
facts.argument: "Hook wounded me... I can neither fly nor swim." ... "To die will be an awfully big adventure."

facts.text: He is described as always sympathetic to the weaker side, clapping when the nest fought and sometimes beat the tide.
facts.argument: "Peter, always sympathetic to the weaker side, could not help clapping" as the nest fought the tide.

facts.text: He basked in the Redskins’ adulation when they called him the Great White Father, which was “not really good for him.”
facts.argument: “They called Peter the Great White Father… and he liked this tremendously, so that it was not really good for him.”

facts.text: Acts as 'Great White Father' toward the Piccaninny, using the phrase 'Peter Pan has spoken' to command silence; left dinner to 'get the time' by finding the ticking crocodile.
facts.argument: "The great white father," he would say...; "Peter Pan has spoken" meant they must now shut up; Peter "had gone out to get the time... find the crocodile".

facts.text: On returning home he is treated as 'father': the children drag him from his tree and ask him to dance. He brings nuts for the boys and the correct time for Wendy, hangs up his gun, is the best dancer (though he feigns 'old bones'), and calls Wendy 'old lady.'
facts.argument: "Children, I hear your father's step"; boys "dragged him from his tree"; "He had brought nuts... and the correct time for Wendy"; "hanging up his gun"; "Peter was really the best dancer... 'My old bones would rattle!'"; "Ah, old lady."

facts.text: He is relieved that being the boys’ father is only make-believe, fearing it would make him seem old; he defines his feelings for Wendy as those of a devoted son.
facts.argument: Peter: “It is only make-believe… that I am their father? … It would make me seem so old…”; “Those of a devoted son, Wendy.”

facts.text: He hates Wendy's story about her parents and usually leaves or covers his ears, but this time he stayed and called for quiet so she could tell it.
facts.argument: "the story Peter hated... Usually when she began to tell this story he left the room or put his hands over his ears... 'Little less noise there,' Peter called out... But to-night he remained on his stool"

facts.text: He reacts with pain to Wendy’s story about mothers and insists she is wrong about them, revealing his distrust of a mother’s constancy.
facts.argument: He “uttered a hollow groan” and told her, “Wendy, you are wrong about mothers.”

facts.text: Tells the boys he once returned home to find his window barred and 'another little boy' in his bed; he believes this story. Angered at grown-ups 'spoiling everything,' he deliberately breathed fast to 'kill' grown-ups per a Neverland saying, and he gave instructions to the Redskins about Wendy’s departure. Though outwardly cool about Wendy leaving, he cared very much.
facts.argument: "the window was barred...another little boy sleeping in my bed"; "Peter thought it was true"; "he was so full of wrath against grown-ups"; "every time you breathe, a grown-up dies"; "having given the necessary instructions to the redskins"; "If you wish it"; "But of course he cared very much"

facts.text: Peter refuses to accompany Wendy back, choosing to stay behind when the others depart.
facts.argument: He tells Wendy, "I am not going with you, Wendy," after allowing the boys to go.

facts.text: Peter speaks with an authoritative, 'short sharp voice' as one accustomed to being obeyed.
facts.argument: "he continued, in the short sharp voice of one accustomed to be obeyed"

facts.text: Refuses to return to London or seek his mother, declaring he wants to remain a little boy and have fun, showing cynicism toward mothers.
facts.argument: Peter: “perhaps she would say I was old, and I just want always to be a little boy and to have fun.” and “If you find your mothers… I hope you will like them.”

facts.text: After the others were taken, Peter tried to act indifferent: he played his pipes, refused to take his medicine to grieve Wendy, lay on top of the coverlet to vex her, laughed a haughty laugh instead of crying, and then fell asleep.
facts.argument: "continued... to play gaily on his pipes... decided not to take his medicine, so as to grieve Wendy... lay down... outside the coverlet, to vex her... he laughed a haughty laugh and fell asleep."

facts.text: Peter sometimes has especially painful dreams and wails piteously in them for hours.
facts.argument: "Sometimes... he had dreams... more painful than the dreams of other boys... For hours he could not be separated from these dreams, though he wailed piteously in them."

facts.text: Keeps a medicine cup by his bed, which was left within reach when he slept.
facts.argument: "Peter's medicine standing on a ledge within easy reach."

facts.text: Upon learning of Wendy's capture, he arms himself and resolves to rescue her.
facts.argument: "I'll rescue her!" he cried, leaping at his weapons.

facts.text: Intending to please Wendy, he decided to take his medicine just before nearly drinking the poisoned draught.
facts.argument: "As he leapt he thought of something he could do to please her. He could take his medicine."

facts.text: Set out at night, armed, on a perilous quest to rescue Wendy; avoided flying low to keep his shadow from alerting foes, advanced with adept native-style stealth, and regretted naming island birds strange names that made them wild and hard to approach amid snow-erased tracks.
facts.argument: "And now to rescue Wendy!"; "begirt with weapons"; "to have flown low would have meant trailing his shadow"; "press forward in redskin fashion, at which... he was an adept"; "he had given the birds... such strange names that they are very wild"; "A light fall of snow had obliterated all footmarks."

facts.text: He taught the children forest lore learned from Tiger Lily and Tinker Bell, expecting Slightly to blaze trees, Curly to drop seeds, and Wendy to leave a handkerchief as clues.
facts.argument: "He had taught the children... forest lore... learned from Tiger Lily and Tinker Bell... Slightly... would blaze the trees... Curly would drop seeds, and Wendy would leave her handkerchief."

facts.text: Realizing the crocodile had fallen silent, he mimicked its tick to pass unmolested; he swam to the Jolly Roger and continued ticking unconsciously.
facts.argument: He "decided to tick, so that wild beasts should believe he was the crocodile"; "reached the shore without mishap"; "went on ticking without knowing that he was doing it."

facts.text: He moved from land into water seemingly without noticing, swimming single-mindedly with the thought, "Hook or me this time."
facts.argument: "His legs encountering the water as if quite unaware... As he swam he had but one thought: 'Hook or me this time.'"

facts.text: Realizes he is imitating the crocodile's ticking and uses it to terrify the pirates while boarding the Jolly Roger.
facts.argument: Peter heard ticking, realized he was doing it himself, and understood the situation; pirates cowered thinking it was the crocodile.

facts.text: Pirates refer to him as the “doodle-doo,” a name tied to his crowing battle-cry.
facts.argument: Hook: “bring me out that doodle-doo.” Cecco calls the killer “the thing you heard crowing.”

facts.text: On the Jolly Roger, Peter found a key in the cabin, freed the children from their manacles, cut Wendy’s bonds, then kept his oath—"Hook or me this time"—by refusing to flee and disguising himself as Wendy to panic the pirates with his crow.
facts.argument: "In the cabin he had found ... the key that would free the children of their manacles"; "Peter cut Wendy's bonds"; "an oath, 'Hook or me this time'"; "took her place by the mast, her cloak around him ... Then he ... crowed"

facts.text: Revealed as the saboteur in the Jolly Roger’s cabin, Peter led the boys into open battle with the command "Down, boys, and at them!", slew Mullins, and then claimed Hook for single combat.
facts.argument: "they all knew who 'twas that had been undoing them in the cabin"; "Down, boys, and at them!"; "who had just passed his sword through Mullins"; "Put up your swords, boys... this man is mine."

facts.text: In the duel with Hook, Peter proves a superb and nimble swordsman, wounding Hook and displaying 'good form' by letting him reclaim his sword; he also declares, "I'm youth, I'm joy... I'm a little bird that has broken out of the egg."
facts.argument: "Peter was a superb swordsman... pierced him in the ribs... invited his opponent to pick up his sword... 'I'm youth, I'm joy... I'm a little bird...'

facts.text: Appears not to know who or what he is; when asked, he replies, "I'm youth, I'm joy... I'm a little bird that has broken out of the egg," which Hook takes as ignorance of self.
facts.argument: "Pan, who and what art thou?" ... "I'm youth, I'm joy... I'm a little bird that has broken out of the egg." "...proof... that Peter did not know in the least who or what he was."

facts.text: Calmly disposed of a live shell by flinging it overboard after emerging from the powder magazine.
facts.argument: "Peter issued from the powder magazine with the shell in his hands, and calmly flung it overboard."

facts.text: After the battle, he had one of his dreams and cried in his sleep for a long time.
facts.argument: "He had one of his dreams that night, and cried in his sleep for a long time."

facts.text: As 'Captain Pan,' he commands the captured Jolly Roger, treating the crew harshly and demanding instant obedience; he consults the chart and sets a course toward the mainland, aiming to reach the Azores around June 21 before flying.
facts.argument: “It need not be said who was the captain… Captain Pan calculated… turned the ship round… treated them as dogs… Instant obedience was the only safe thing.”

facts.text: After Wendy began sewing him a new suit from Hook’s garments, it was whispered he sat in the cabin with Hook’s cigar-holder and held his forefinger aloft like a hook, echoing Hook’s manner.
facts.argument: “It was afterwards whispered… first night he wore this suit… cigar-holder… forefinger… like a hook.”

facts.text: Plots and executes a trick to keep Wendy by barring the Darling nursery window so she will think her mother rejected her and go back with him, ignoring Mrs. Darling’s tears.
facts.argument: "Quick Tink, close the window; bar it!... when Wendy comes she will think her mother has barred her out; and she will have to go back with me." He sees her tears but says, "I won't" unbar it.

facts.text: Boasts about his mother despite knowing nothing about her, comparing Mrs. Darling unfavourably.
facts.argument: "Of course he knew nothing whatever about his mother; but he sometimes bragged about her... not so pretty as my mother."

facts.text: Relented and unbarred the Darling nursery window to let Wendy, John, and Michael return, then flew off with Tinker Bell declaring they didn't want mothers.
facts.argument: "Then he unbarred the window. 'Come on, Tink,' ... 'we don't want any silly mothers;' and he flew away."

facts.text: Watches the Darling family reunion from the window, recognizing it as a joy forever denied to him.
facts.argument: A "little boy" stared in at the window... looking at "the one joy from which he must be for ever barred."

facts.text: Declines adoption and rejects schooling and manhood; plans to live with Tinker Bell in the little house the fairies will set high in the treetops.
facts.argument: "Would you send me to school?... I don't want to be a man." / "With Tink in the house we built for Wendy. The fairies are to put it high up among the tree tops..."

facts.text: Has no sense of time, is absorbed in recounting his own adventures, and forgets past foes and friends—asking "Who is Captain Hook?" and "Who is Tinker Bell?" and remarking, "I forget them after I kill them."
facts.argument: "He had no sense of time... he had so much to say about himself... 'Who is Captain Hook?'... 'I forget them after I kill them'... 'Who is Tinker Bell?'

facts.text: Peter missed a year’s visit and, when he returned at next spring cleaning, he did not know a year had passed; he stayed away for years afterward and next met Wendy when she was already married.
facts.argument: “Peter came next spring cleaning; and the strange thing was that he never knew he had missed a year… when they met again Wendy was a married woman.”

facts.text: He is said to be never ill.
facts.argument: Michael: “Perhaps he is ill.” Wendy: “You know he is never ill.”

facts.text: Peter returns unchanged as a little boy with all his first teeth, expects Wendy to fly away for spring cleaning, does not grasp that she has grown up, and reacts with fear and pain before breaking down in tears.
facts.argument: “He was exactly the same as ever… still had all his first teeth… ‘Are you expecting me to fly away?’ ‘Of course… spring cleaning time’… ‘Don’t turn up the light’… he gave a cry of pain… and sobbed.”

facts.text: Returns to take Jane as his 'mother' for spring cleaning and later continues with her daughter Margaret, coming each spring (except when he forgets) and eagerly listening to stories about himself.
facts.argument: "I came back for my mother... to take her to the Neverland."; "It is just for spring cleaning time"; later: "every spring cleaning time, except when he forgets, Peter comes for Margaret... where she tells him stories about himself, to which he listens eagerly."

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: The narrative personifies the stars with intentions and sentiments: they wink, watch, and are described as being on Peter's side tonight though usually not friendly to him.

facts.text: They cannot take an active part, only watch; winking is their language; the older stars are glassy-eyed, while the little ones still wonder.
facts.argument: "Stars... may not take an active part... must just look on"; "winking is the star language"; "older ones have become glassy-eyed... little ones still wonder."

facts.text: On this night, they crowded around the Darling house, curious, and some smaller stars winked at Mrs. Darling.
facts.argument: "They were crowding round the house... one or two of the smaller ones winked at her."

facts.text: The smallest star in the Milky Way prompts Peter to act, shouting "Now, Peter!"
facts.argument: "the smallest of all the stars in the Milky Way screamed out: 'Now, Peter!'"

summaries.text: Personified celestial beings who observe events and communicate through winks. Generally unfriendly to Peter Pan for his antics, they show curiosity towards the Darling house, with older stars being glassy-eyed and younger ones still filled with wonder.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: A fairy enters the nursery, flashing like light, no longer than a hand, called Tinker Bell; she speaks in a tinkling-bell fairy language and helps Peter look for his shadow.

facts.text: Was accidentally shut in a drawer by Peter; emerged furious, screamed, briefly rested on the cuckoo clock; speaks insulting, bell-like fairy language; identified as a 'tinker' fairy who mends pots and kettles.
facts.argument: "I do believe I shut her up in the drawer!"; "flew about the nursery screaming with fury"; rested "on the cuckoo clock"; "that's the fairy language"; "she is called Tinker Bell because she mends the pots and kettles."

facts.text: Tinker Bell shows jealousy and hostility toward Wendy, pulling her hair when Peter gives Wendy a 'thimble' and using offensive language.
facts.argument: Wendy screeches as if hair pulled; Peter says it must have been Tink; Tink darts about using offensive language and threatens to do it every time Peter gives a thimble.

facts.text: During the approach to Neverland, their straight course was attributed less to her guidance than to the island "looking for them."
facts.argument: "not perhaps so much owing to the guidance of Peter or Tink as because the island was looking for them."

facts.text: Acts as Peter’s scout; she was asleep on his shoulder until he woke her and sent her on ahead.
facts.argument: “Tinker Bell had been asleep on his shoulder, but now he wakened her and sent her on in front.”

facts.text: At this moment Tink is 'all bad,' consumed by jealousy of Wendy; she pops out of the hat and tries to lure Wendy to her destruction, reflecting a fairy's single, all-consuming feeling at a time.
facts.argument: "she at once popped out of the hat and began to lure Wendy to her destruction... At present she was full of jealousy of Wendy... Fairies... have room for one feeling only at a time."

facts.text: Jealous of Wendy, she openly abandoned any pretense of friendship, physically attacked Wendy, and told the boys "Peter wants you to shoot the Wendy."
facts.argument: Described as "The jealous fairy" who was "pinching savagely" and shouted, "Peter wants you to shoot the Wendy."

facts.text: Temporarily banished by Peter for a week for her crime; she pleaded on his shoulder but was brushed off.
facts.argument: "I am your friend no more... Well, not for ever, but for a whole week." She flew to his shoulder and pleaded; he brushed her off.

facts.text: Lives in a private recess in the underground home; fastidious about privacy (keeps a tiny curtain drawn when dressing); maintains a lavishly furnished fairy-scale boudoir and lights it herself; contemptuous of the rest of the house.
facts.argument: “one recess… the private apartment of Tinker Bell… tiny curtain… Tink… always kept drawn when dressing”; “Her mirror was a Puss‑in‑Boots… chandelier from Tiddlywinks… of course she lit the residence herself”; “Tink was very contemptuous of the rest of the house.”

facts.text: Plotted with street fairies to send sleeping Wendy to the mainland on a great floating leaf; the plan failed when the leaf gave way and Wendy swam back.
facts.argument: “Tinker Bell's attempt, with the help of some street fairies, to have the sleeping Wendy conveyed on a great floating leaf to the mainland. Fortunately the leaf gave way and Wendy ... swam back.”

facts.text: Openly proclaims she “glories in being abandoned,” rejects any motherly role toward Peter, and bluntly insults him (“You silly ass!”).
facts.argument: Peter: “She says she glories in being abandoned.”; Tink: “You silly ass!”

facts.text: Has her own bedroom in the underground home and is prone to eavesdropping on conversations, responding with impudent remarks.
facts.argument: “Tink, who was in her bedroom, eavesdropping, squeaked out something impudent.”

facts.text: Drank the poisoned draught intended for Peter and is now critically weak, saying she is "going to be dead."
facts.argument: "with ... lightning movements Tink ... drained it to the dregs"; "it was poisoned ... now I am going to be dead"

facts.text: Overheard Hook muttering about poisoning Peter’s medicine as he sped through the forest.
facts.argument: "who had heard Hook mutter about his deed as he sped through the forest."

facts.text: Near death, she was revived when distant children clapped to show belief in fairies after Peter's plea; she sprang up stronger, more merry and impudent than ever, did not thank believers, and wanted to get at those who had hissed.
facts.argument: "If you believe... clap your hands; don't let Tink die" ... "but already Tink was saved"; "more merry and impudent than ever"; "She never thought of thanking those who believed... would have like to get at the ones who had hissed."

facts.text: Plans to live with Peter in the little house that the fairies will set among the treetops.
facts.argument: Peter: "With Tink in the house we built for Wendy. The fairies are to put it high up among the tree tops..."

facts.text: Her status after the Darlings' return is uncertain; Peter no longer remembers her and says, "I expect she is no more," with the narrator noting fairies don't live long.
facts.argument: Peter: "Who is Tinker Bell?" and "I expect she is no more"; narrator adds fairies have short lives.

summaries.text: Tinker Bell is a tiny, still-growing fairy girl allied with Peter Pan. She flashes like light when moving, speaks in tinkling-bell fairy language, wears a skeleton-leaf dress, and is associated with fairy dust.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Peter explains he mostly lives with them and is their captain; they are boys who fell from perambulators and were sent to Neverland if unclaimed.

facts.text: Peter portrays the boys as lacking a mother’s care and basic clothing needs: they have never been tucked in at night, have no pockets, and need their clothes darned; he seeks someone (Wendy) to tell them stories.
facts.argument: "None of us has ever been tucked in at night"; "And you could darn our clothes, and make pockets for us. None of us has any pockets"; "do come with me and tell the other boys."

facts.text: At this time the band numbers six (counting the Twins as two). They are out to greet Peter, go single-file with daggers, are forbidden by Peter to resemble him, and wear self-slain bear skins that make them round and sure-footed.
facts.argument: "there were six of them, counting the twins as two"; "The lost boys were out looking for Peter... out to greet their captain"; "each with his hand on his dagger"; "forbidden by Peter to look in the least like him"; "wear the skins of the bears slain by themselves"

facts.text: As a rule they like blood, but tonight they were not seeking it and were out to greet their captain Peter.
facts.argument: "All wanted blood except the boys, who liked it as a rule, but to-night were out to greet their captain."

facts.text: The Lost Boys have an underground home; they collapse nearby on the sward, nervous of the pirates and wishing for Peter’s return, though they are mostly bigger than Peter.
facts.argument: "The first to fall out... flung themselves down... close to their underground home. 'I do wish Peter would come back,' every one of them said nervously... though... they were all larger than their captain."

facts.text: Their underground home is accessed via seven tree trunks with boy-sized holes; the boys drop into these to hide swiftly when danger (e.g., pirates) approaches.
facts.argument: "seven large trees, each with a hole... These are the seven entrances to the home under the ground... Rabbits could not have disappeared more quickly."

facts.text: At this time there are seven Lost Boys, implied by the seven tree-trunk entrances and Hook's intent to "mischief all the seven."
facts.argument: "seven large trees... These are the seven entrances"; Hook: "I want to mischief all the seven."

facts.text: Their underground home has seven entrances via tree-trunk holes, and Hook speaks of 'all the seven' boys to target; this refers to entrances/targets here and does not alter the known size of the Lost Boys group.
facts.argument: "seven large trees... These are the seven entrances to the home"; Hook: "I want to mischief all the seven."

facts.text: Their underground home has a chimney disguised as a removable mushroom, which they customarily plug when enemies are nearby.
facts.argument: "They had indeed discovered the chimney of the home under the ground... It was the custom of the boys to stop it with a mushroom when enemies were in the neighbourhood."

facts.text: Their underground home appears to consist of a single room served by one chimney, with multiple entrances above.
facts.argument: Hook deduces: "There can be but one room below, for there is but one chimney... The silly moles had not the sense to see that they did not need a door apiece."

facts.text: They follow Peter's perceived orders without question, acting immediately on commands relayed by others.
facts.argument: "It was not in their nature to question when Peter ordered."

facts.text: They recognized Wendy as a "lady" meant to take care of them.
facts.argument: "A lady to take care of us at last," said one of the twins; "Peter was bringing her to us," said Curly.

facts.text: Initially mistook Wendy for a bird and referred to her as "the Wendy."
facts.argument: "Let us do what Peter wishes!... I have shot the Wendy."

facts.text: They declare themselves Wendy’s servants, call her "the Wendy," and gut their own house to furnish a little house built around her (chairs and a fender first).
facts.argument: "For the Wendy," said Curly… "That is why we are her servants." Peter: "Gut our house… Chairs and a fender first; then we shall build a house round them."

facts.text: They construct a cosy little house for Wendy using red-sapped branches and moss, punching out windows and using yellow leaves as blinds, and make-believe roses and babies.
facts.argument: "branches... sticky with red sap... ground was carpeted with moss"; "With a blow of their fists they made windows, and large yellow leaves were the blinds"; "Quickly they made-believe to grow the loveliest roses... The babes are at the door."

facts.text: Kneel and adopt Wendy as their mother, asking her to mother them.
facts.argument: "Then all went on their knees... 'O Wendy lady, be our mother.'"

facts.text: The Lost Boys’ underground home is a single large room with stout mushrooms used as stools; a central Never tree is sawed daily—its two-foot stump, topped with a door at tea-time, serves as a table, then is cut again for play space. Access is via individual hollow trees fitted to each child, using breath control to descend/ascend.
facts.argument: "It consisted of one large room... stout mushrooms... A Never tree tried hard to grow... they sawed the trunk... put a door on top... becoming a table... to descend you drew in [let out] your breath... you simply must fit, and Peter measures you for your tree."

facts.text: In the underground home they sleep packed together in a single bed let down at night, following a strict ‘turning’ signal; they rely on Wendy’s domestic care and often dine on make‑believe meals depending on Peter’s whim.
facts.argument: “the bed… all the boys slept in it… rule against turning round until one gave the signal”; “Wendy stretched strings… suspended her washing… cooking… you never exactly knew whether… a real meal or just a make‑believe… it all depended upon Peter’s whim.”

facts.text: Their tree‑trunk entrances fit their bodies; diet is regulated so that if a boy is getting ‘loose’ for his tree, Peter allows him to stodge.
facts.argument: “if you could prove to him that you were getting loose for your tree he let you stodge.”

facts.text: The Lost Boys eagerly joined Wendy’s examinations, made their own slates, and are so hard on their knees that Wendy double-reinforces their clothing.
facts.argument: “The other boys… insisted on joining, and they made slates for themselves… putting double pieces on the knees, for they were all most frightfully hard on their knees.”

facts.text: The Lost Boys often insist adventures are wholly true even when only partly true.
facts.argument: “there were still more that were at least partly true, for the other boys were in them and said they were wholly true.”

facts.text: At Peter's command to dive, the Lost Boys instantly vanished into the lagoon, obeying without question.
facts.argument: "'Dive!' There was a gleam of legs, and instantly the lagoon seemed deserted."

facts.text: They mischievously tossed treasure from a discovered hoard—moidores, diamonds, pearls, and pieces of eight—to gulls, and later, after returning home hours late, demanded bandages to stay up and played at limping and wearing slings.
facts.argument: “The children had discovered the glittering hoard… used to fling showers of moidores… to the gulls… Great were the rejoicings… they were several hours late for bed… demanding bandages… they played… at limping… and carrying their arms in slings.”

facts.text: During make-believe teas they are noisy and quarrelsome, subject to Wendy’s rule to file disputes as formal complaints, which they often forget or overuse.
facts.argument: "make-believe tea"; "the noise... was positively deafening"; "They... should refer the matter... by raising the right arm... but... forgot to do this or did it too much."

facts.text: The boys frequently bicker and tattle during meals, calling out each other's small offenses.
facts.argument: "The hateful telling broke out again... 'Slightly is coughing'... 'Curly is taking both butter and honey'... 'I complain of the twins'... 'I complain of Curly'... 'I complain of Nibs.'

facts.text: Under Wendy and Peter’s domestic routine, the boys put on their nighties before being allowed to dance on ‘Saturday night.’
facts.argument: “So they were told they could dance, but they must put on their nighties first.”

facts.text: When they want to do something special, the household calls it “Saturday night,” having lost track of days.
facts.argument: “They had long lost count of the days; but… if they wanted to do anything special they said this was Saturday night.”

facts.text: They love Wendy's good-night story about her parents and eagerly listen in bed.
facts.argument: "the story they loved best"; "seven boys in the bed"

facts.text: They delight in Wendy’s tale while showing callousness toward parents’ feelings, trusting in a mother’s love to excuse their absence.
facts.argument: They “moaned... though they were not really considering the feelings of the unhappy parents”; “So great indeed was their faith in a mother’s love... they felt they could afford to be callous.”

facts.text: Panic-stricken at losing Wendy, they advanced on her, vowing not to let her go, proposing to keep her prisoner and "chain her up." They believed one can "get on quite well without a mother."
facts.argument: "We shan't let her go" ... "Let's keep her prisoner" ... "Ay, chain her up" ... "they knew ... one can get on quite well without a mother"

facts.text: The Lost Boys decide to leave Neverland with Wendy to be adopted by her parents, eagerly preparing to depart.
facts.argument: They "jumped with joy" at Wendy's promise of adoption and "immediately... rushed to get their things."

facts.text: Slightly's tree door has a low catch (child-height), which adults like Hook cannot reach from inside, hindering intruders.
facts.argument: Hook finds "the door of Slightly's tree" and the catch "low down, beyond his reach."

facts.text: Captured by the pirates and taken aboard their ship.
facts.argument: "she told of the capture of Wendy and the boys"

facts.text: On the Jolly Roger, as the pirates prepared the plank, the Lost Boys went white, could only stare and shiver; after Wendy’s last words, they echoed a resolve to die 'like English gentlemen.'
facts.argument: They "went white" and "could stare and shiver only"; after Wendy’s speech they repeated, "What my mother hopes."

facts.text: Freed from manacles by Peter aboard the Jolly Roger, the Lost Boys hid and armed themselves with whatever weapons they could find.
facts.argument: "the key that would free the children of their manacles ... they all stole forth, armed ... First signing them to hide"

facts.text: During the melee on the Jolly Roger, the Lost Boys hunted pirates in pairs, choosing isolated targets; they surrounded Hook while Slightly assisted by blinding hiding pirates with a lantern.
facts.argument: "they fought on the defensive only, which enabled the boys to hunt in pairs and choose their quarry"; "a group of savage boys surrounded Hook"; Slightly’s lantern tactic described.

facts.text: After the battle, they operate the captured Jolly Roger like a crew; by three bells they were all up working the ship, with Tootles serving as boatswain.
facts.argument: "By three bells that morning they were all stirring... and Tootles, the bo'sun, was among them."

facts.text: They suspect Peter’s present honesty is to lull Wendy’s suspicions and later whispered he mimicked Hook after donning his new suit.
facts.argument: “general feeling was that Peter was honest just now to lull Wendy’s suspicions… afterwards whispered… held forefinger… like a hook.”

facts.text: After seizing the Jolly Roger, they donned pirate clothes and served as common sailors (“tars”) living in the fo’c’sle; opinions split between making the ship honest or keeping it pirate, though they suppressed this under Peter’s command.
facts.argument: “They all donned pirate clothes… The rest were tars before the mast, and lived in the fo’c’sle… Some of them wanted it to be an honest ship and others were in favour of keeping it a pirate.”

facts.text: Return with Wendy to the Darling home, respectfully present themselves (hats off, still in pirate clothes) and seek adoption; reassure Mr. Darling they will 'fit in.'
facts.argument: They 'stood in a row... with their hats off... wishing they were not wearing their pirate clothes'; 'their eyes asked her to have them' and 'We'll fit in, sir.'

facts.text: Six of the Lost Boys present themselves for adoption at the Darling house, prompting Mr. Darling to consider 'six a rather large number.'
facts.argument: Mr. Darling "considered six a rather large number" when the boys stood before them.

facts.text: Adopted into the Darling family by Mrs. Darling.
facts.argument: "She told Peter that she had adopted all the other boys..."

facts.text: After returning, the boys went to school, settled into ordinary lives, and gradually lost the power to fly as their belief faded.
facts.argument: "Of course all the boys went to school... soon they settled down to being as ordinary... It is sad... the power to fly gradually left them... what it really meant was that they no longer believed."

facts.text: Soon after starting school, they regretted not remaining in Neverland but eventually settled into ordinary life.
facts.argument: "Before they had attended school a week they saw what goats they had been not to remain on the island... and soon they settled down to being as ordinary..."

facts.text: All the boys eventually grew up and were “done for,” taking ordinary adult roles in the world.
facts.argument: “All the boys were grown up and done for by this time… You may see the twins and Nibs and Curly… Slightly… Tootles…”

summaries.text: A group of boys in Neverland who fell out of their perambulators and, if unclaimed in seven days, were sent away to defray expenses. Led by Peter Pan, they live with him and have no girls among them.

The Lost Boys are a group of boys in Neverland, led by Peter Pan, who were abandoned and lack maternal care. They have no girls among them and are characterized by their need for basic clothing and nurturing, seeking Wendy for stories and comfort.

The Lost Boys are a group of six boys in Neverland, led by Peter Pan. Abandoned and lacking maternal care, they seek comfort and stories from Wendy. They wear self-slain bear skins, have no pockets, and live in an underground home, often nervous of pirates.

The Lost Boys are a group of six boys in Neverland, led by Peter Pan. Abandoned and lacking maternal care, they wear self-slain bear skins and live in an underground home with seven tree trunk entrances, often nervous of pirates and seeking stories from Wendy.

The Lost Boys are a group of six boys in Neverland, led by Peter Pan. Abandoned and lacking maternal care, they wear self-slain bear skins and live in an underground home with seven tree trunk entrances, often nervous of pirates and seeking stories from Wendy.

The Lost Boys are a group of six boys in Neverland, led by Peter Pan. Abandoned and lacking maternal care, they wear self-slain bear skins and live in an underground home with seven tree trunk entrances, often seeking stories from Wendy and nervous of pirates.

The Lost Boys are a group of six boys in Neverland, led by Peter Pan. Abandoned and motherless, they wear bear skins and live in an underground home with seven tree trunk entrances. They seek stories from Wendy and are wary of pirates, viewing her as a maternal figure.

The Lost Boys, led by Peter Pan, are a group of six motherless boys in Neverland, living in an underground home with seven tree trunk entrances. They view Wendy as a maternal figure, seeking her stories and care, while being wary of pirates.

The Lost Boys, led by Peter Pan, are a group of seven motherless boys in Neverland, living in an underground home with seven tree trunk entrances. They view Wendy as a maternal figure, seeking her care and stories, while being wary of pirates.

The Lost Boys, led by Peter Pan, are seven motherless boys in Neverland, living in an underground home with tree trunk entrances. They view Wendy as a maternal figure, seeking her care and stories, while being wary of pirates and following Peter's commands without question.

The Lost Boys, led by Peter Pan, are seven motherless boys in Neverland, living in an underground home accessed through tree trunks. They view Wendy as a maternal figure, eagerly seeking her care and stories, while following Peter's commands and evading pirates.

The Lost Boys, led by Peter Pan, are seven motherless boys in Neverland, living in an underground home accessed through tree trunks. They view Wendy as a maternal figure, eagerly seeking her care and stories, while following Peter's commands and evading pirates.
