facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "And, Wendy, there are mermaids." "Mermaids! With tails?" "Such long tails."

facts.text: Mermaids bask on Marooners' Rock and play rainbow-bubble games after rain, but they avoid and tease Wendy and the boys by diving and splashing them. They are friendly with Peter, chatting for hours and letting him sit on their tails. At the turn of the moon they utter strange wailing cries, and they adopted John's head-hitting method for bubbles.
facts.argument: “they loved to bask… on Marooners’ Rock”; “except of course Peter, who chatted with them… and sat on their tails”; “utter strange wailing cries”; “after rain… bubbles… the mermaids adopted it [John’s head hit].”

facts.text: Mermaids retire to bedchambers under the sea; each coral cave door rings a tiny bell when opening/closing; their calls to the moon are the most musical yet melancholy sound.
facts.argument: "the mermaids retiring... to their bedchambers... every door in the coral caves... rings a tiny bell... the mermaids calling to the moon."

summaries.text: Mermaids of Neverland, described as having long tails; their existence entices Wendy with the prospect of seeing them.

The Mermaids of Neverland are enchanting beings with long tails, known for basking on Marooners' Rock and teasing Wendy and the boys. They are friendly with Peter Pan, engaging in playful chats, and are known for their eerie wailing cries at the moon's turn.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "And there are pirates."

facts.text: Known for a recurring dreadful song, heard before they are seen: "Avast belay, yo ho, heave to... A‑pirating we go..."
facts.argument: "We hear them before they are seen, and it is always the same dreadful song: 'Avast belay... A-pirating we go...'"

facts.text: Hook's crew is a notorious, villainous lot, including Cecco, Bill Jukes, Cookson, Gentleman Starkey, Smee, Noodler, Robert Mullins, Alf Mason, and the now-dead Skylights, among other ruffians feared on the Spanish Main.
facts.argument: "A more villainous-looking lot... Here is Bill Jukes... Cookson... Gentleman Starkey... Skylights... Smee... Noodler... Robt. Mullins and Alf Mason and many another ruffian long known and feared on the Spanish Main."

facts.text: Their approach is marked by a grim marching song about the pirate life and Davy Jones.
facts.argument: "Yo ho, yo ho, the pirate life... And hey for Davy Jones."

facts.text: Hook and Smee discover the Lost Boys' underground home's chimney disguised as a removable mushroom and note the holes in seven trees nearby, then replace the mushroom.
facts.argument: "A chimney!"; "They had indeed discovered the chimney of the home under the ground... they noted the holes in the seven trees."

facts.text: The pirates could be heard carousing far away at night near the boys’ home.
facts.argument: "for the pirates could be heard carousing far away"

facts.text: The pirates use Marooners' Rock to maroon enemies at high tide, as shown by their plan to drown Tiger Lily there.
facts.argument: "what we have to do is to hoist the redskin on to it and leave her here to drown."

facts.text: Following Hook, the pirates ignored the usual pre-dawn waiting tactics and pushed an immediate attack instead of holding position.
facts.argument: Hook’s usual-procedure was known; he "would not even hold off"; pirates advanced with him to attack at once.

facts.text: Pirates massacred many Piccaninny braves by surprise but lost crew including Alf Mason, George Scourie, Charles Turley, and the Alsatian Foggerty; afterwards they kept a discreet distance from Hook’s hook, wary.
facts.argument: Casualties listed: "with Lean Wolf fell Alf Mason... Geo. Scourie, Chas. Turley, and the Alsatian Foggerty"; "they gathered at a discreet distance from his hook."

facts.text: During the capture, the pirates trussed the children with their knees to their ears and gagged them to prevent escape by flight.
facts.argument: "They were tied to prevent their flying away, doubled up with their knees close to their ears" and "where the others were being gagged."

facts.text: On a quiet night aboard the Jolly Roger, some pirates leaned over the bulwarks breathing the night miasma, others gambled with dice and cards, while four exhausted from carrying the little house lay prone on deck.
facts.argument: "A few of the pirates leant over the bulwarks... others sprawled by barrels over games of dice and cards; and the exhausted four who had carried the little house lay prone on the deck."

facts.text: Believing the crocodile was boarding, they did not fight it, treating it as Fate, and they hid Hook.
facts.argument: "They had no thought of fighting it. It was Fate." and "The pirates respectfully cleared a passage for him... Hide me!"

facts.text: The crew grow unnerved by the eerie crowing and show mutinous signs when Hook hesitates to re-enter the dark cabin.
facts.argument: “The exultation of the boys, the lowering looks of the pirates… His reluctance to return to the cabin… and the mutinous sounds again broke forth.”

facts.text: The pirates displayed deep superstition, fearing an unaccounted presence as a 'Jonah,' panicking at Peter’s crow, and invoking Flint’s saying that a woman on board brings bad luck.
facts.argument: "There's a Jonah aboard"; panic after the crow; "Never was luck on a pirate ship wi' a woman on board"; "this had been a saying of Flint's."

facts.text: In the sudden melee on the Jolly Roger, the pirates panicked and scattered; though stronger man-to-man, they fought defensively, with some leaping into the sea and others hiding in recesses.
facts.argument: "Had the pirates kept together it is certain that they would have won... they ran hither and thither... Man to man they were the stronger; but they fought on the defensive... Some... leapt into the sea; others hid in dark recesses."

facts.text: Defeated aboard the Jolly Roger: fifteen pirates killed; only Smee and Gentleman Starkey reached the shore.
facts.argument: "Fifteen paid the penalty for their crimes that night; but two reached the shore: Starkey... and Smee."

summaries.text: A group of pirates in Neverland; their mention excites John to leave immediately and promises adventure and conflict.
A group of pirates in Neverland, known for their dreadful song "Avast belay, yo ho, heave to... A-pirating we go..." Their mention excites John, promising adventure and conflict.

A notorious group of pirates in Neverland, known for their dreadful song "Avast belay, yo ho, heave to... A-pirating we go..." Led by Captain Hook, their crew includes Cecco, Bill Jukes, Smee, and others, instilling fear across the Spanish Main.

A notorious group of pirates in Neverland, led by Captain Hook, includes Cecco, Bill Jukes, Smee, and others. Known for their dreadful song "Avast belay, yo ho, heave to... A-pirating we go...", they instill fear across the Spanish Main and are infamous for their villainous deeds.

Led by Captain Hook, the notorious pirates of Neverland include Cecco, Bill Jukes, Smee, and others. Infamous for their villainous deeds and the dreadful song "Avast belay, yo ho, heave to... A-pirating we go...", they instill fear across the Spanish Main.

Led by Captain Hook, the notorious pirates of Neverland, including Cecco, Bill Jukes, and Smee, are infamous for their villainous deeds and the dreadful song "Avast belay, yo ho, heave to... A-pirating we go..." They instill fear across the Spanish Main.

Led by Captain Hook, the notorious pirates of Neverland, including Smee, Cecco, and Bill Jukes, are infamous for their villainous deeds and the dreadful song "Avast belay, yo ho, heave to... A-pirating we go..." They instill fear across the Spanish Main.

Led by Captain Hook, the infamous pirates of Neverland, including Smee, Cecco, and Bill Jukes, are known for their villainous deeds and the dreadful song "Avast belay, yo ho, heave to... A-pirating we go..." They instill fear across the Spanish Main.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "a million golden arrows were pointing it out to the children, all directed by their friend the sun, who wanted them to be sure of their way before leaving them for the night."

facts.text: Guided the children to Neverland by directing a million golden arrows at the island before setting for the night.
facts.argument: "a million golden arrows were pointing it out... all directed by their friend the sun, who wanted them to be sure of their way before leaving them for the night."

facts.text: As its guiding arrows depart (sunset), the island falls into gloom, heralding a fearful time.
facts.argument: “It came as the arrows went, leaving the island in gloom.”

summaries.text: The Sun is a personified celestial guide who directs golden arrows to help travelers find their way, notably guiding children to Neverland before setting for the night. Introduced in c21, it symbolizes warmth and direction.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "not perhaps so much owing to the guidance of Peter or Tink as because the island was looking for them"; the children recognized it at once as a familiar friend.

facts.text: The island actively "looked for" the travelers, enabling them to go straight and be able to sight its magic shores; on first sight it feels like a familiar friend.
facts.argument: "because the island was looking for them"; "It is only thus that any one may sight those magic shores"; the children "hailed it... as a familiar friend."

facts.text: At night Neverland grows dark and threatening; unseen hostile forces in the air resist landings and slow flight until forcefully pushed through.
facts.argument: “leaving the island in gloom… over the fearsome island… slow and laboured… as if pushing through hostile forces… Peter had beaten on it with his fists… ‘They don’t want us to land.’”

facts.text: Features visible from the air include a lagoon, the Mysterious River, pampas, and wildlife such as wolves with whelps and turtles nesting in the sand.
facts.argument: “there’s the lagoon… across the Mysterious River… a wolf with her whelps… turtles burying their eggs… a pirate asleep in the pampas.”

facts.text: The island feels real and dangerous at night; unlike at home, there are no night-lights or Nana for comfort.
facts.argument: “the Neverland had been make-believe in those days, but it was real now, and there were no night-lights… and where was Nana?”

facts.text: Stirs to intense, island-wide activity when Peter approaches; factions circle the island at the same speed without meeting.
facts.argument: "Feeling that Peter was on his way back, the Neverland had again woke into life... They were going round and round the island, but they did not meet because all were going at the same rate."

facts.text: At night the island's inhabitants move in a continuous circular pursuit along an often invisible war-path; each party stalks the next until someone stops or changes pace, so danger often comes from behind.
facts.argument: "stealing noiselessly down the war-path, which is not visible to inexperienced eyes... the procession must continue indefinitely until one of the parties stops or changes its pace... none suspects that the danger may be creeping up from behind."

facts.text: In Neverland, space seems unusually accommodating—you can "squeeze very tight," allowing many to fit into small places like the little house.
facts.argument: "I don't know how there was room for them, but you can squeeze very tight in the Neverland."

facts.text: Time is loosely tracked on the island; when they want to do something special, they call it Saturday night regardless of the actual day.
facts.argument: “They had long lost count of the days; … they said this was Saturday night, and then they did it.”

summaries.text: Neverland is a magical island that actively seeks out travelers, making it feel instantly familiar to arriving children, like a beloved place. It is characterized by its enchanting shores and the ability to guide children directly to its wonders.

Neverland is a magical island that beckons travelers, especially children, making it feel like a familiar friend. By day, it boasts enchanting shores and wonders, but at night, it transforms into a dark, threatening place with unseen dangers and no comforts.

Neverland is a magical island that attracts children with its enchanting shores by day, but becomes dark and threatening at night, filled with unseen dangers. It actively seeks travelers, featuring a lagoon, wildlife, and intense activity when Peter Pan is near.

Neverland is a magical, enchanting island that attracts children by day but becomes dark and threatening at night, filled with unseen dangers. It features a lagoon, wildlife, and stirs to life with intense activity when Peter Pan is near, actively seeking travelers.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “I say, John, I see the smoke of the redskin camp!” / “Yes, they are on the war-path right enough.”

facts.text: Their camp smoke is seen across the Mysterious River; smoke curl indicates they are on the war-path.
facts.argument: “I see the smoke of the redskin camp… just across the Mysterious River… Yes, they are on the war-path right enough.”

facts.text: In Peter's absence they feed heavily for six days and nights; tonight they are out looking for the pirates.
facts.argument: "the redskins feed heavily for six days and nights"; "the redskins were out looking for the pirates"

facts.text: The Piccaninny tribe stalks the pirates along the war-path, moving noiselessly with tomahawks and knives; they wear scalps of boys as well as pirates, and after recent gorging they breathe heavily.
facts.argument: "On the trail of the pirates... come the redskins... for these are the Piccaninny tribe... Strung around them are scalps, of boys as well as of pirates... pass over fallen twigs without making the slightest noise... The only sound... heavy breathing... they are all a little fat... after the heavy gorging."

facts.text: The tribe holds that there is no path through water to the happy hunting-ground, making death by drowning especially terrible.
facts.argument: "is it not written in the book of the tribe that there is no path through water to the happy hunting-ground?"

facts.text: After Peter saved Tiger Lily, the tribe befriended Peter and the boys; they kept nightly watch over the underground home, smoked the pipe of peace by day, and called Peter the “Great White Father,” prostrating themselves before him.
facts.argument: “It made the redskins their friends… All night they sat above, keeping watch… Even by day they hung about, smoking the pipe of peace… They called Peter the Great White Father, prostrating themselves before him.”

facts.text: Stand watch in their blankets above the children's home, protecting Peter’s "wigwam" from pirates and deferring when he declares, "Peter Pan has spoken."
facts.argument: They were "protecting his wigwam from the pirates"; "the redskins in their blankets were at their posts above"; they accepted it humbly when he said "Peter Pan has spoken."

facts.text: Night tactics: scouts wriggle silently through the grass, imitate the lonely coyote call, and braves wear moccasins with the heels in front to mask tracks; with alert senses they detect intruders by the slightest sound.
facts.argument: Scouts "wriggle, snake-like"; they give the coyote cry; braves wear "mocassins with the heels in front"; they knew pirates were on the island when one "trod on a dry stick."

facts.text: Suffered heavy losses in a surprise massacre by the pirates; their tradition of never showing surprise before whites delayed their initial response.
facts.argument: "they remained stationary... It is written that the noble savage must never express surprise in the presence of the white... Thus perished many of the flower of the Piccaninny tribe."

facts.text: Beating the tom-tom is the Redskins' customary sign of victory.
facts.argument: "If the redskins have won," Peter said, "they will beat the tom-tom; it is always their sign of victory."

summaries.text: The Redskins are a native group in Neverland, known for their camp smoke that reveals their movements. Currently, they are on the war-path, with their smoke visible across the Mysterious River.

The Redskins are a native group in Neverland, recognized by their camp smoke that signals their movements. Currently on the war-path, they stalk pirates with tomahawks and knives, wearing scalps as trophies, and are known for their heavy breathing after feasting.

The Redskins are a native tribe in Neverland, known for their camp smoke signaling war-paths. They stalk pirates with tomahawks, wearing scalps as trophies, and breathe heavily after feasting. They once befriended Peter Pan, calling him the 'Great White Father'.

The Redskins are a native tribe in Neverland, known for their stealthy war tactics and smoke signaling. They once befriended Peter Pan, calling him the 'Great White Father,' and protect his home from pirates, wearing scalps as trophies.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Peter identifies the pirates' current captain as Hook ("Jas. Hook"), a feared figure whom Peter says he maimed.

facts.text: Current captain of the pirates in Neverland; formerly Blackbeard's boatswain and reputedly feared even by 'Barbecue'.
facts.argument: Peter says Hook is captain; John adds, "He was Blackbeard's bo'sun... the only man of whom Barbecue was afraid."

facts.text: Lost his right hand to Peter Pan and now has an iron hook which he uses to claw; feared by the Darling children.
facts.argument: Peter says, "I cut off a bit of him...His right hand... He has an iron hook instead of a right hand, and he claws with it," causing Michael to cry and John to gulp.

facts.text: Commands his crew from a rough chariot they draw; treats them like dogs and goads them with his iron hook; smokes two cigars at once via a self-made holder; cadaverous and dark-faced with long black curls; blue, melancholic eyes that ignite with red spots when he strikes; elegant, grand-seigneur manner and reputed raconteur; indomitable courage yet shies at sight of his own thick, unusually colored blood; affects Charles II attire; styles his name "Jas. Hook."
facts.argument: "reclined... in a rough chariot drawn... As dogs this terrible man treated and addressed them... holder... smoke two cigars at once... cadaverous and blackavized... hair... eyes... two red spots... grand seigneur... RACONTEUR... only thing he shied at was the sight of his own blood, which was thick and of an unusual colour... aped the attire... Charles II... as he wrote himself, Jas. Hook."

facts.text: Reputed to be the only man the Sea-Cook feared, underscoring his fearsome legend.
facts.argument: "of whom it is said he was the only man that the Sea-Cook feared."

facts.text: Has long searched in vain for the Lost Boys' underground entrances; forbids gunfire to avoid alerting Tiger Lily's redskins; intends to harm all the boys.
facts.argument: "for which Hook has been searching in vain these many moons"; "Put back that pistol... the sound would have brought Tiger Lily's redskins upon us"; "I want to mischief all the seven."

facts.text: Hook's voice is described as "black."
facts.argument: "Now for the first time we hear the voice of Hook. It was a black voice."

facts.text: Peter Pan cut off Hook's arm and flung it to a crocodile; that crocodile has pursued Hook ever since. It swallowed a ticking clock that warns Hook of its approach, and he fears the day it runs down.
facts.argument: "'Twas he cut off my arm... Peter flung my arm... to a crocodile... it has followed me ever since"; "it swallowed a clock which goes tick tick... before it can reach me I hear the tick and bolt"; "that's the fear that haunts me."

facts.text: He is proud of his iron hook, claiming it is better than a hand, and uses it for combing hair and other homely tasks; he scorns his remaining natural hand.
facts.argument: Smee: you say the hook is "worth a score of hands, for combing the hair and other homely uses." Hook: "if I was a mother I would pray to have my children born with this instead of that," casting pride on the iron hand and scorn on the other.

facts.text: Devises a plan to kill the Lost Boys by baking a large rich cake with green sugar and leaving it at the Mermaids' Lagoon, counting on their lack of a mother; he infers their lair has only one room and one chimney.
facts.argument: "cook a large rich cake... with green sugar... We will leave the cake on the shore of the Mermaids' Lagoon... That shows they have no mother... There can be but one room below, for there is but one chimney."

facts.text: Scoffed at the boys for thinking they needed a separate hollow tree each, revealing his ignorance of how the entrances must fit their sizes.
facts.argument: "Hook, you remember, had sneered at the boys for thinking they needed a tree apiece, but this was ignorance"

facts.text: Hook boasts that the wind of his name guards the pirate ship for a mile around, so he keeps no watch.
facts.argument: "No watch was kept on the ship, it being Hook's boast that the wind of his name guarded the ship for a mile around."

facts.text: Arrived swimming and sat in melancholy, then declared, "The game's up—those boys have found a mother," treating the boys’ mother (Wendy) as a dire threat.
facts.argument: He sat with his head on his hook... "The game's up," he cried, "those boys have found a mother."

facts.text: Momentarily broken when taunted as a “codfish,” losing the men’s confidence, but on hearing Peter Pan’s name he recovered command, ordered Peter taken dead or alive, and fought so fiercely with his iron claw that the boys fled his deadly circle.
facts.argument: “A codfish!” … “his proud spirit broke … his men draw back.” … “Pan! In a moment Hook was himself again … ‘Take him dead or alive!’ … “His iron claw made a circle of dead water … they fled like affrighted fishes.”

facts.text: Shows a self-analytical, intuitive side—“a touch of the feminine”—that led him to test the unseen voice with a guessing game.
facts.argument: “In his dark nature there was a touch of the feminine … it sometimes gave him intuitions. Suddenly he tried the guessing game.”

facts.text: After Peter aided him, Hook bit and twice clawed Peter with his iron hook, then fled in white fear with the Crocodile in pursuit.
facts.argument: "Hook bit him... Twice the iron hand clawed him... only white fear, for the crocodile was in dogged pursuit of him."

facts.text: Captain Hook is referred to as the 'Sea-Cook,' a moniker used when noting he feared Peter Pan.
facts.argument: "he was the only man that the Sea-Cook had feared."

facts.text: Disregards the usual pre-dawn waiting procedure and treacherously drives an immediate attack, refusing to wait to be attacked.
facts.argument: "Disregarding it he cannot be excused"; he "would not even hold off till the night was nearly spent"; "on he pounded with no policy but to fall to [get into combat]."

facts.text: Used a surprise ambush on Tiger Lily’s warriors as a means to reach Peter Pan; his true target was chiefly Peter (whom he hates), though he also sought Wendy and the Lost Boys.
facts.argument: "They were but the bees to be smoked... It was Pan he wanted, Pan and Wendy and their band, but chiefly Pan... one tends to wonder at the man's hatred of him."

facts.text: Peter Pan's cockiness specifically goads Hook to frenzy; it makes his iron claw twitch and torments him at night.
facts.argument: "It was Peter's cockiness... it made his iron claw twitch, and at night it disturbed him like an insect."

facts.text: Hook orders a deception using the Indians' tom-tom and arranges an ambush: one pirate at each tree, others in a line two yards apart.
facts.argument: "Hook signed him to beat the tom-tom... Rapidly and silently Hook gave his orders: one man to each tree, and the others to arrange themselves in a line two yards apart."

facts.text: From Slightly's altered tree, Hook inferred Peter was at his mercy and formed a plan to make a foul attempt on Peter's life; he ordered the captives sent to the ship and remained behind alone.
facts.argument: "Sufficient of this Hook guessed to persuade him that Peter at last lay at his mercy" and "without the secret he could not presently have made his foul attempt on Peter's life" and he "signed that the captives were to be conveyed to the ship, and that he would be alone."

facts.text: Displaying ruthless ingenuity, Hook orders the little house used as a conveyance to transport the captured children through the wood.
facts.argument: "Hook's genius surmounted difficulties. He indicated that the little house must be used as a conveyance... the procession set off through the wood."

facts.text: He always carries a homemade, highly virulent yellow poison (blended from death-dealing rings) and used it to poison Peter's medicine.
facts.argument: "Hook always carried ... a dreadful drug... boiled down into a yellow liquid... Five drops of this he now added to Peter's cup."

facts.text: Despite his villainy, he loves flowers and sweet music and is a capable harpsichord player.
facts.argument: "The man was not wholly evil; he loved flowers ... and sweet music (he was himself no mean performer on the harpsichord)."

facts.text: Secretly poisoned Peter Pan’s medicine and fled through the forest, muttering about his deed.
facts.argument: "who had heard Hook mutter about his deed as he sped through the forest"; "The cup was poisoned."

facts.text: Hook’s name is an alias; he was educated at a famous public school, its traditions still clinging to him, and revealing his true identity would "set the country in a blaze."
facts.argument: "Hook was not his true name ... he had been at a famous public school ... to reveal who he really was would even at this date set the country in a blaze; and its traditions still clung to him."

facts.text: Despite triumph, Hook often paces the deck at night profoundly dejected and terribly alone, feeling socially superior to his crew.
facts.argument: "It was his hour of triumph ... Hook was profoundly dejected ... This inscrutable man never felt more alone than when surrounded by his dogs. They were socially inferior to him."

facts.text: Hook is obsessively governed by the notion of 'good form' instilled at his school; he still keeps the school's distinguished slouch and hears an inner school voice judging him, and he even restrains himself (e.g., not clawing Smee) to avoid 'bad form.'
facts.argument: "he retained the passion for good form… adhered… to the school's distinguished slouch"; "Have you been good form to-day?"; "To claw a man because he is good form… Bad form!"

facts.text: On the Jolly Roger, Hook ordered the boys to walk the plank and sought to make Wendy watch their deaths.
facts.argument: "Bring up their mother. Get the plank ready." and "His intention was to turn her face so that she should see the boys walking the plank one by one."

facts.text: Hook’s ruff was soiled, and he self-consciously tried to hide it when he noticed Wendy looking.
facts.argument: "the intensity of his communings had soiled his ruff"; he "knew that she was gazing at it" and "tried to hide it."

facts.text: Paralyzed by the ticking he thought was the crocodile, he crawled away and begged to be hidden; even his iron claw hung inactive.
facts.argument: "The iron claw hung inactive"; he "crawled... as far from the sound as he could go" and cried "Hide me!"

facts.text: Emerges unsteadily from the dark cabin claiming something blew out his lantern and shows reluctance to return, unsettling the crew.
facts.argument: “Something blew out the light,” he said a little unsteadily… His reluctance to return to the cabin… mutinous sounds broke forth.

facts.text: Shows rare fear and hesitation—staggering from the dark cabin and avoiding return—which undermines his authority and emboldens mutiny.
facts.argument: “Hook came staggering out… ‘Something blew out the light’ … His reluctance to return… and the mutinous sounds again broke forth.”

facts.text: Despite losing heart upon realizing Peter had undone them, Hook fought ferociously, keeping multiple boys at bay, hewing space around him, and even using a boy lifted on his hook as a shield.
facts.argument: "twice Hook essayed to speak and twice he failed... his fierce heart broke"; "he kept them at bay in that circle of fire... again and again he hewed a clear space... lifted up one boy with his hook, and was using him as a buckler"

facts.text: His favourite thrust was taught to him long ago by one called Barbecue at Rio, but Peter repeatedly turned it aside.
facts.argument: "a favourite thrust, taught him long ago by Barbecue at Rio; but... found this thrust turned aside again and again."

facts.text: Seeing his own peculiarly coloured blood—offensive to him—made his sword fall from his hand after Peter pierced him in the ribs.
facts.argument: "At the sight of his own blood, whose peculiar colour... was offensive to him, the sword fell from Hook's hand."

facts.text: Obsessed with 'good form'; he interprets Peter’s self-ignorance as the pinnacle of good form and longs, even in despair, to witness Peter show bad form.
facts.argument: "with a tragic feeling that Peter was showing good form"; "proof... that Peter did not know... which is the very pinnacle of good form"; "for one boon it craved: to see Peter show bad form."

facts.text: In desperate defeat he abandons the duel, rushes to the powder magazine, and ignites it to blow up the Jolly Roger within two minutes.
facts.argument: "Abandoning the fight he rushed into the powder magazine and fired it. 'In two minutes... the ship will be blown to pieces.'

facts.text: Dies by leaping to the sea where the crocodile awaits; accepts a final kick from Peter and jeers 'Bad form' before perishing.
facts.argument: "Bad form," he cried jeeringly, and went content to the crocodile. Thus perished James Hook.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "The first to pass is Tootles, not the least brave but the most unfortunate..." He is described as humble, unlucky, and often missing adventures.

facts.text: Often misses major adventures by stepping away to gather firewood, returning after the action; his ill-luck has made him humbly sweet and gently melancholy.
facts.argument: "big things constantly happened just when he had stepped round the corner... going off to gather a few sticks for firewood... when he returned the others would be sweeping up the blood... given a gentle melancholy... sweetened it... quite the humblest of the boys."

facts.text: Considered the most easily tricked of the boys by Tinker Bell, who seeks to use him as a tool for mischief tonight.
facts.argument: "Tink... is looking for a tool... and she thinks you are the most easily tricked of the boys."

facts.text: Says he is confident his mother must have been very like Cinderella.
facts.argument: "They talked of Cinderella, and Tootles was confident that his mother must have been very like her."

facts.text: Shot Wendy with an arrow after Tinker Bell's prompting; initially proud but then remorseful, taking responsibility with new-found dignity.
facts.argument: "I have shot the Wendy... Peter will be so pleased"; later, "I did it," he said, trembling yet dignified.

facts.text: Yearns for a mother; in dreams he called visiting ladies "Pretty mother," revealing his longing for maternal care.
facts.argument: "When ladies used to come to me in dreams, I said, 'Pretty mother, pretty mother.'"

facts.text: Accepted blame and knelt, baring his breast and inviting Peter to strike him for shooting Wendy, showing humble courage.
facts.argument: “Mine, Peter”… “Strike, Peter… strike true.” He “bared his breast.”

facts.text: Before Peter arrived, he tried to leave, admitting he was afraid of Peter.
facts.argument: “He moved slowly away… ‘I must… I am so afraid of Peter.’”

facts.text: Expresses urgent concern for Wendy’s life after the shooting, warning she will die if left lying there.
facts.argument: Tootles said, "But if she lies there, she will die."

facts.text: Gave the sole of his shoe to serve as a door knocker for Wendy's house.
facts.argument: "Tootles gave the sole of his shoe, and it made an excellent knocker."

facts.text: Wounded in the lagoon fight when Smee’s corkscrew cutlass struck him in the fourth rib.
facts.argument: “The corkscrew of Smee got Tootles in the fourth rib.”

facts.text: Often scapegoated by the boys during meals; they excuse grabbing by claiming Tootles pushed their elbows.
facts.argument: They excused grabbing "by saying that Tootles had pushed their elbow."

facts.text: So self-effacing that he begs for any role (father, then baby, then a twin) and even offers to do a trick, but is refused each time, ending with resigned acceptance.
facts.argument: "I could be father"—"No"; "be baby?"—"No"; "be a twin?"—"No"; "see me do a trick?"—"No" … "I hadn't really any hope."

facts.text: He knows Wendy's story by heart.
facts.argument: "'It's awfully puzzling,' said Tootles, who knew the story by heart."

facts.text: He delights in being included in Wendy’s story, excitedly asking if one of the lost children was named Tootles and celebrating, “I am in a story.”
facts.argument: “O Wendy… was one of the lost children called Tootles?” … “Hurrah, I am in a story.”

facts.text: When Wendy appealed to him, he dropped his silliness, spoke with dignity, and threatened to "blood" any boy who failed to behave to Wendy "like an English gentleman," drawing back his hanger so the others held back.
facts.argument: "'Tootles,' she cried, 'I appeal to you.'"; "'the first who does not behave to Wendy like an English gentleman I will blood him severely.'"; "He drew back his hanger; ... The others held back"

facts.text: To avoid provoking Hook, he stepped forward politely but cited his mother's disapproval as a reason not to join the pirates.
facts.argument: "Don't irritate him unnecessarily" ... Tootles: "I don't think my mother would like me to be a pirate."

facts.text: In hysterics on the Jolly Roger, Tootles vowed to do what his mother hoped—die like an English gentleman.
facts.argument: "Tootles cried out hysterically, 'I am going to do what my mother hopes.'"

facts.text: After the battle, he serves as the Jolly Roger's boatswain, carrying a rope's end and chewing tobacco.
facts.argument: "Tootles, the bo'sun, was among them, with a rope's end in his hand and chewing tobacco."

facts.text: Tootles became a judge.
facts.argument: “You see that judge in a wig…? That used to be Tootles.”

summaries.text: Tootles, a Lost Boy, is the humblest and most unlucky of the group, often missing major adventures due to his ill-luck. Known for his gentle melancholy, he is easily tricked by Tinker Bell, who uses him for mischief.

Tootles, a Lost Boy, is the humblest and most unlucky of the group, often missing adventures due to his ill-luck. Easily tricked by Tinker Bell, he yearns for maternal care and shows gentle melancholy, taking responsibility after shooting Wendy with an arrow.

Tootles, a humble Lost Boy, is known for his ill-luck and gentle melancholy. Easily tricked by Tinker Bell, he yearns for maternal care and shows courage after accidentally wounding Wendy. He often misses adventures and is scapegoated by the other boys.

Tootles, a gentle and ill-fated Lost Boy, is easily tricked by Tinker Bell and yearns for maternal care. He shows courage after accidentally wounding Wendy and often misses adventures, being scapegoated by the other boys. He serves as the Jolly Roger's boatswain post-battle.

Tootles, a gentle and ill-fated Lost Boy, is easily tricked by Tinker Bell and yearns for maternal care. He shows courage after accidentally wounding Wendy and often misses adventures, being scapegoated by the other boys. He later serves as the Jolly Roger's boatswain.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "In his absence things are usually quiet on the island. The fairies take an hour longer in the morning..." establishing the fairy folk as a group entity in Neverland.

facts.text: In Peter's absence they linger, taking an hour longer in the morning; their activity quickens on his return.
facts.argument: "In his absence things are usually quiet... The fairies take an hour longer in the morning"

facts.text: Fairies hold nocturnal orgies and tend to play mischief on boys who obstruct their path at night.
facts.argument: "unsteady fairies... on their way home from an orgy. Any of the other boys obstructing the fairy path at night they would have mischiefed"

facts.text: Fairies' vitality can depend on children's belief; applause from believing children revived Tinker Bell from the brink of death.
facts.argument: "She thought she could get well again if children believed in fairies" and the clapping saved Tink.

facts.text: New fairies are born when a baby laughs for the first time; they live and sleep in nests on treetop tops. Mauve fairies are boys, white are girls, and blue are undecided little sillies.
facts.argument: Wendy explains: first baby laugh births a fairy; they live in nests on tops of trees; mauve=boys, white=girls, blue=not sure.

facts.text: Fairies have short lifespans; being so small, even a brief span seems long to them.
facts.argument: "I expect he was right, for fairies don't live long, but they are so little that a short time seems a good while to them."

summaries.text: The Fairies of Neverland are magical beings whose energy and routines slow when Peter Pan is absent and quicken upon his return, reflecting their deep connection to him.

The Fairies of Neverland are magical beings whose energy is tied to Peter Pan; they slow down in his absence and quicken upon his return. Their vitality relies on children's belief, and they engage in mischief and nocturnal gatherings.

The Fairies of Neverland are magical beings linked to Peter Pan, whose vitality depends on children's belief. They engage in mischief, hold nocturnal gatherings, and are born from a baby's first laugh, with mauve fairies as boys, white as girls, and blue as undecided.

The Fairies of Neverland are magical beings tied to Peter Pan, thriving on children's belief. They are born from a baby's first laugh, with mauve fairies as boys, white as girls, and blue as undecided. They engage in mischief and nocturnal gatherings.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "the beasts attend to their young" and later "the beasts were out looking for the redskins" establish the wild animals as a force on the island.

facts.text: In Peter's absence they attend to their young; tonight they are out looking for the Redskins.
facts.argument: "the beasts attend to their young"; "the beasts were out looking for the redskins"

facts.text: After the redskins, a motley procession of beasts (lions, tigers, bears, and others) passes, tongues hanging out; on the island, especially the man-eaters, they live cheek by jowl and are hungry tonight.
facts.argument: "their place is taken by the beasts: lions, tigers, bears... Their tongues are hanging out, they are hungry to-night... all the man-eaters, live cheek by jowl on the favoured island."

facts.text: Wolves prowl at night around the area of the boys’ home, posing a danger.
facts.argument: "the wolves were on the prowl"

facts.text: Some beasts hissed when distant children clapped to save Tinker Bell.
facts.argument: "Many clapped. Some didn't. A few beasts hissed."

summaries.text: The Beasts are wild animals of Neverland, known for their protective nature towards their young in Peter Pan's absence. They become predatory towards the Redskins when the island is stirred, showcasing their fierce instincts.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "there were six of them, counting the twins as two" identifies a distinct pair within the Lost Boys.

facts.text: Inseparable and indistinguishable; keep close together apologetically and remain vague about themselves because Peter didn’t know what twins were and forbade his band to know what he didn’t.
facts.argument: "Last come the Twins... cannot be described... these two were always vague... keeping close together... Peter never quite knew what twins were, and his band were not allowed to know anything he did not know,"

facts.text: One twin declared Wendy was "a lady to take care of us at last" and blamed Tootles for killing her.
facts.argument: "A lady to take care of us at last," said one of the twins, "and you have killed her!"

facts.text: Initially helped conceal Wendy from Peter, then stepped back when Tootles told them to let Peter see.
facts.argument: “Hide her…,” and later, “Back, twins, let Peter see.”

facts.text: Declared themselves Wendy's children when she emerged from the house.
facts.argument: "And we are your children," cried the twins."

facts.text: The first twin is the proud one; he speaks up to ask if they'd be too much of a handful, showing sensitivity to being singled out.
facts.argument: "The first twin was the proud one, and he asked... 'Do you think we should be too much of a handful, sir?'"

facts.text: As adults, the Twins go to an office daily, each carrying a little bag and an umbrella.
facts.argument: “You may see the twins… going to an office, each carrying a little bag and an umbrella.”

summaries.text: A pair within the Lost Boys, simply called the Twins; counted as two of the six boys at this time.

The Twins are inseparable members of the Lost Boys, known for their indistinguishability and vague identities. Introduced in [c25], they stay close together, adhering to Peter Pan's rules, as he was unaware of twins and forbade his band from knowing what he didn't.

The Twins are indistinguishable members of the Lost Boys, introduced in [c25]. They are inseparable and vague about their identities due to Peter Pan's ignorance of twins. One twin is proud and sensitive, while they both declare themselves Wendy's children.

The Twins are indistinguishable members of the Lost Boys, introduced in [c25]. They are inseparable, vague about their identities due to Peter Pan's ignorance of twins, with one being proud and sensitive. They declare themselves Wendy's children and later lead adult lives.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "Next comes Nibs, the gay and debonair"

facts.text: Described as gay and debonair among the Lost Boys.
facts.argument: "Next comes Nibs, the gay and debonair"

facts.text: Acts as a scout, darting away to reconnoitre when pirates approach; recalls his mother wishing for a cheque-book and longs to give her one though he doesn't know what it is.
facts.argument: "with the exception of Nibs, who has darted away to reconnoitre"; "All I remember... she often said... 'I wish I had a cheque-book of my own!'... I should just love to give my mother one."

facts.text: Pursued by a pack of wolves at night, he fled breathlessly and cried for help before falling to the ground.
facts.argument: "Nibs rushed breathless... pursued by a pack of wolves... 'Save me, save me!'... falling on the ground."

facts.text: First to spot Wendy in the sky, he mistook her for a "great white bird" moaning "Poor Wendy."
facts.argument: "A great white bird. It is flying this way... it looks so weary, and as it flies it moans, 'Poor Wendy.'"

facts.text: Noticed Wendy move her arm and reverently thought he heard her say, “Poor Tootles.”
facts.argument: “It is she… the Wendy lady, see, her arm!”; “I think she said, ‘Poor Tootles.’”

facts.text: Urged Wendy to be pleased with the house the boys built.
facts.argument: "Oh, say you're pleased," cried Nibs."

facts.text: During make-believe meals he tattles and corrects others, e.g., pointing out Slightly hadn’t begun his milk.
facts.argument: "He hasn't even begun to drink his milk," Nibs interposed.

facts.text: Serves as first mate under Captain Pan aboard the Jolly Roger.
facts.argument: “Nibs and John were first and second mate.”

facts.text: Shows willingness to accommodate by offering to 'lie doubled up' to fit into the Darling home.
facts.argument: "We could lie doubled up," said Nibs.

facts.text: Nibs now goes to an office, carrying a little bag and an umbrella.
facts.argument: “You may see the twins and Nibs and Curly any day going to an office, each carrying a little bag and an umbrella.”

summaries.text: Nibs, a Lost Boy from Peter Pan, is characterized as gay and debonair, often seen following Peter in the boys' procession. He stands out among the Lost Boys for his charming demeanor.

Nibs, a debonair Lost Boy from Peter Pan, is known for his charming demeanor and loyalty to Peter. He serves as first mate on the Jolly Roger, acts as a scout, and is characterized by his longing for his mother and his mistaken admiration for Wendy.

Nibs, a debonair Lost Boy from Peter Pan, is known for his charm, loyalty to Peter, and longing for his mother. He serves as first mate on the Jolly Roger, acts as a scout, and mistakenly admires Wendy, mistaking her for a bird and urging her approval of the boys' house.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "Slightly, who cuts whistles out of the trees and dances ecstatically to his own tunes... Slightly is the most conceited of the boys... He thinks he remembers the days before he was lost... and this has given his nose an offensive tilt."

facts.text: Cuts whistles from trees and dances ecstatically to his own tunes; the most conceited Lost Boy, claiming to remember pre-lost days with their manners and customs, giving his nose an "offensive tilt."
facts.argument: "Slightly, who cuts whistles out of the trees and dances ecstatically to his own tunes... Slightly is the most conceited of the boys... He thinks he remembers the days before he was lost... and this has given his nose an offensive tilt."

facts.text: Boasts he alone is unafraid of the pirates, then quickly backtracks and admits he wants Peter to return with news about Cinderella.
facts.argument: "'I am the only one who is not afraid of the pirates,' Slightly said... then hastily, 'but I wish he would come back, and tell us whether he has heard anything more about Cinderella.'"

facts.text: Claimed there are birds called "Wendies," then recognized the figure was a lady, not a bird.
facts.argument: "there are birds called Wendies"; later: "This is no bird... I think this must be a lady."

facts.text: Claimed to ‘remember kisses’ and identified Peter’s button as a kiss.
facts.argument: “I remember kisses… Ay, that’s a kiss.”

facts.text: Claims knowledge of etiquette and building, remarking "that is what one does with ladies" and "that is how a house is built; it all comes back to me."
facts.argument: Slightly: "That is what one does with ladies" … "Ay… that is how a house is built; it all comes back to me."

facts.text: Slightly pretends to be a doctor by donning John's hat, make-believes to examine/cure Wendy with a 'glass thing,' then returns the hat and blows big breaths; he is noted to have chapped knuckles.
facts.argument: "fetch a doctor" ... Slightly returned wearing John's hat; "I will put a glass thing in her mouth"; later "after he had returned the hat to John he blew big breaths"; "who had chapped knuckles."

facts.text: While impersonating the doctor, he deliberately 'does not see' Wendy lying at his feet to maintain the make-believe scenario.
facts.argument: "She was lying at their feet, but Slightly had the sense not to see her."

facts.text: First to speak to Wendy after the house is finished, declaring it was built for her.
facts.argument: "Slightly was the first to get his word in. 'Wendy lady,' he said rapidly, 'for you we built this house.'"

facts.text: Slightly replied to every question on Wendy’s exam and expected to come first, but his answers were ridiculous and he actually came last.
facts.argument: “the only boy who replied to every question was Slightly… his answers were perfectly ridiculous, and he really came out last.”

facts.text: Addresses Wendy as "mummy" and plays along with make-believe meals (checking an imaginary mug), promptly using the complaint protocol against Nibs.
facts.argument: "Not quite empty, mummy," after looking into an imaginary mug; "I complain of Nibs," he cried promptly.

facts.text: He attempted to tell a story but found his beginning so dull that he proposed pretending it was the end.
facts.argument: "Even Slightly tried to tell a story... 'Yes, it is a dull beginning. I say, let us pretend that it is the end.'"

facts.text: Addicted to drinking water when hot, he swelled and secretly whittled his tree to fit his size, leaving him panicked about Peter and regretful.
facts.argument: "Madly addicted to the drinking of water when he was hot, he had swelled...and...had...whittled his tree to make it fit him" and he was "in a panic about Peter, bitterly regretted what he had done."

facts.text: Slightly's tree serves as a passable entrance to the underground home, which Hook is able to use to infiltrate.
facts.argument: "Slightly's tree... provided him with a passage... He stepped into the tree... He arrived... in the home under the trees."

facts.text: The door of his tree has a low-placed catch and does not fully fill the aperture, hindering tall intruders like Hook from opening it from inside.
facts.argument: Hook encounters "the door of Slightly's tree" with the catch "low down, beyond his reach," and the door "did not entirely fill the aperture."

facts.text: Slightly’s tree has a “dark secret” unknown to Tinker Bell.
facts.argument: "even she did not know the dark secret of Slightly's tree."

facts.text: If given the chance, he leaves blazed marks on trees to guide others.
facts.argument: "Slightly, if he had an opportunity, would blaze the trees."

facts.text: Keeps tally aloud during the attack, marking events with curt counts: “Two,” “Three,” “Four,” “Five.”
facts.argument: Slightly solemnly: “Two.” Later: “Three.” … “Four.” … “Five.”

facts.text: Counts aloud during the boarding fight—“Two,” “Three,” “Four”—and longs to say “Five” but refrains when Hook reappears.
facts.argument: Slightly: “Two.” Later: “Three.” … “Four.” Then: “How Slightly longed to say it … but Hook came staggering out.”

facts.text: During the battle aboard the Jolly Roger, Slightly did not fight with a sword; he ran with a lantern, blinding hiding pirates so others could dispatch them, all while counting the fallen.
facts.argument: "Slightly, who did not fight, but ran about with a lantern... flashed in their faces... fell as an easy prey... Slightly monotonously counting—five—six—seven..."

facts.text: Miscounted the pirates' casualties, calling out "Seventeen" when only fifteen died.
facts.argument: "'Seventeen,' Slightly sang out; but he was not quite correct in his figures. Fifteen paid the penalty..."

facts.text: At school he was demoted from Class IV to Class V while most others were placed in Class III.
facts.argument: "Most of them got into Class III, but Slightly was put first into Class IV and then into Class V."

facts.text: Slightly married a lady of title and thereby became a lord.
facts.argument: “Slightly married a lady of title, and so he became a lord.”

summaries.text: Slightly, the most conceited Lost Boy, is known for cutting whistles from trees and dancing to his own tunes. He claims to remember pre-lost days, which gives him an 'offensive tilt' in demeanor.

Slightly, the conceited Lost Boy, is known for whittling whistles and dancing to his own tunes. He claims to remember pre-lost days, often boasting about his knowledge of etiquette and pretending to be a doctor, while addressing Wendy as 'mummy'.

Slightly, the conceited Lost Boy, is known for whittling whistles and pretending to be a doctor. He boasts about his pre-lost memories and addresses Wendy as 'mummy.' His antics include ridiculous claims and a penchant for etiquette, often leading to humorous situations.

Slightly, the conceited Lost Boy, is known for whittling whistles and pretending to be a doctor. He boasts about pre-lost memories, addresses Wendy as 'mummy,' and often finds himself in humorous situations due to his ridiculous claims and etiquette pretensions.

Slightly, the conceited Lost Boy, is known for whittling whistles and pretending to be a doctor. He addresses Wendy as 'mummy,' boasts of pre-lost memories, and often finds himself in humorous situations due to his ridiculous claims and etiquette pretensions.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "Curly is fourth; he is a pickle... so often has he had to deliver up his person when Peter said sternly, 'Stand forth the one who did this thing,' that now... he stands forth automatically."

facts.text: A "pickle" often singled out when Peter demands the culprit; now stands forth automatically at the command, even when innocent.
facts.argument: "Curly is fourth; he is a pickle... so often has he had to deliver up his person when Peter said sternly, 'Stand forth the one who did this thing,' that now... he stands forth automatically whether he has done it or not."

facts.text: Identified Wendy in the sky and concluded Peter was bringing her to the boys.
facts.argument: "See, it comes!"; later: "Now I see: Peter was bringing her to us."

facts.text: Observed that Tinker Bell was crying because Wendy lived, implying he recognized Tink’s jealousy toward Wendy.
facts.argument: “Listen to Tink,” said Curly, “she is crying because the Wendy lives.”

facts.text: Proposes carrying Wendy down into the house, takes Peter’s order to direct the boys, and explains they are Wendy’s servants.
facts.argument: "Let us carry her down into the house," Curly suggested… Peter: "Curly, see that these boys help…" Curly: "That is why we are her servants."

facts.text: Fought back in the lagoon melee, ‘pinking’ Smee after Tootles was stabbed.
facts.argument: “… but he [Smee] was himself pinked in turn by Curly.”

facts.text: Michael and Curly previously tried to have the kite lift two people, which failed.
facts.argument: "It can't lift two; Michael and Curly tried."

facts.text: Curly is the first Lost Boy to emerge from his tree during the ambush.
facts.argument: "The first to emerge from his tree was Curly."

facts.text: He would drop seeds to mark a trail for others to follow.
facts.argument: "Curly would drop seeds."

facts.text: Expressed patriotic support during the standoff by squeaking "Rule Britannia!"
facts.argument: "Rule Britannia!" squeaked Curly.

facts.text: Curly now goes to an office, carrying a little bag and an umbrella.
facts.argument: “You may see the twins and Nibs and Curly any day going to an office, each carrying a little bag and an umbrella.”

summaries.text: Curly, a Lost Boy often singled out by Peter Pan, automatically steps forward when accused, even if innocent. His tendency to find himself in predicaments highlights his unique role within the group.

Curly, a Lost Boy from Peter Pan's group, is often singled out for blame, stepping forward automatically when accused. He is observant, recognizing Wendy and Tinker Bell's dynamics, and shows leadership by directing the boys and marking trails. Curly now carries an umbrella and bag to his office.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "the handsome Italian Cecco... his great arms bare, pieces of eight in his ears as ornaments... cut his name in letters of blood on the back of the governor of the prison at Gao"

facts.text: During the march he repeatedly puts his head to the ground to listen, acting as a scout.
facts.argument: "ever and again with his head to the ground listening"

facts.text: Cecco helped prepare the fatal plank for the boys.
facts.argument: "Jukes and Cecco preparing the fatal plank."

facts.text: Dies in the dark cabin aboard the Jolly Roger during the boys' attack, after entering to fetch the 'doodle-doo.'
facts.argument: Hook: “Go back and fetch me out that doodle-doo.” … Later: “He’s as dead as Jukes,” said Hook shortly.

summaries.text: Cecco is a handsome Italian pirate in Hook's crew, recognized for wearing pieces of eight as earrings and his brutal past of carving his name in blood on a prison governor at Gao. He also acts as a scout, listening to the ground during marches.

Cecco is a handsome Italian pirate in Hook's crew, known for wearing pieces of eight as earrings and his brutal past of carving his name in blood. He serves as a scout, listening to the ground during marches, and dies in the dark cabin of the Jolly Roger during an attack.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "Here is Bill Jukes, every inch of him tattooed... who got six dozen on the WALRUS from Flint before he would drop the bag of moidores"

facts.text: Jukes helped prepare the fatal plank for the boys.
facts.argument: "Jukes and Cecco preparing the fatal plank."

facts.text: Dies aboard the Jolly Roger, found stabbed in the dark cabin during the boys' attack.
facts.argument: “The matter wi' him is he's dead, stabbed,” replied Cecco… “The cabin's as black as a pit.”

summaries.text: Bill Jukes is a heavily tattooed pirate in Hook's crew, flogged "six dozen" on the WALRUS by Flint before surrendering stolen moidores.

Bill Jukes is a heavily tattooed pirate in Captain Hook's crew, known for being flogged by Flint and for preparing the fatal plank for the boys. He is recognized for his tough demeanor and loyalty to Hook.

Bill Jukes is a heavily tattooed pirate in Captain Hook's crew, known for his tough demeanor and loyalty to Hook. He helped prepare the fatal plank for the boys and died aboard the Jolly Roger, found stabbed in the dark cabin during their attack.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "and Cookson, said to be Black Murphy's brother (but this was never proved)"

facts.text: Cookson showed superstitious fear and insolence toward Hook, taunting, "Had he a hook, captain?" while declaring the ship accurst if someone unaccounted was aboard.
facts.argument: "They do say the surest sign a ship's accurst is when there's one on board more than can be accounted for"; "'Had he a hook, captain?' asked Cookson insolently"

summaries.text: Cookson is a pirate in Hook's crew, rumored (but unproven) to be Black Murphy's brother.

Cookson is a pirate in Hook's crew, rumored to be Black Murphy's brother. He exhibits superstitious fear and insolence towards Hook, famously taunting him about his hook and declaring the ship cursed if someone unaccounted is aboard.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "and Gentleman Starkey, once an usher in a public school and still dainty in his ways of killing"

facts.text: Shows a quick eye; spotted Nibs and attempted to shoot him before Hook restrained him.
facts.argument: "the quick eye of Starkey sighted Nibs... his pistol flashed out. But an iron claw gripped his shoulder."

facts.text: Starkey accompanied Smee in the dinghy and helped land Tiger Lily on Marooners' Rock to drown.
facts.argument: "the pirate dinghy, with three figures in her, Smee and Starkey... It was the work of one brutal moment to land the beautiful girl on the rock"

facts.text: Displays nervous obedience to Hook; urged compliance with the 'captain’s' orders and later exclaimed, "O evil day!" upon learning the boys have a mother.
facts.argument: "Better do what the captain orders," said Starkey nervously; later, "O evil day!"

facts.text: He had hung his deep tarpaulin hat on the stave at the lagoon; afterward he often watched bitterly as the Never Bird sat on his hat until it went to pieces.
facts.argument: “On it Starkey had hung his hat… often Starkey came to the shore of the lagoon… watched the bird sitting on his hat… It drifted about till it went to pieces.”

facts.text: Leapt overboard into the sea to avoid entering the dark cabin after Hook’s coercion during rising mutiny.
facts.argument: “With a despairing scream the pirate leapt upon Long Tom and precipitated himself into the sea.”

facts.text: Survives the battle and reaches shore but is captured by the Redskins and made nurse to their papooses.
facts.argument: "Starkey to be captured by the redskins, who made him nurse for all their papooses."

summaries.text: Gentleman Starkey is a pirate in Hook's crew; formerly a public school usher, he remains daintily precise even in killing.
Gentleman Starkey is a precise pirate in Hook's crew, formerly a public school usher. He has a keen eye for targets, as shown when he attempted to shoot Nibs before being restrained by Hook.

Gentleman Starkey is a precise pirate in Hook's crew, formerly a public school usher. Known for his keen eye, he attempted to shoot Nibs and shows nervous obedience to Hook, often urging compliance with orders. He also helped land Tiger Lily on Marooners' Rock.

Gentleman Starkey is a precise pirate in Hook's crew, formerly a public school usher. Known for his keen eye and nervous obedience to Hook, he attempted to shoot Nibs and helped land Tiger Lily on Marooners' Rock, later becoming a captive nurse to the Redskins.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "and Skylights (Morgan's Skylights)"

summaries.text: Skylights, also called Morgan's Skylights, is a pirate in Hook's crew.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "the Irish bo'sun Smee, an oddly genial man who stabbed, so to speak, without offence, and was the only Non-conformist in Hook's crew"

facts.text: Calls his cutlass "Johnny Corkscrew" (which he wiggles in the wound), gives pleasant names to things, wipes his spectacles after killing instead of his weapon, and is described as rather stupid.
facts.argument: "Johnny Corkscrew... because he wiggled it in the wound"; "Smee had pleasant names for everything"; "after killing, it was his spectacles he wiped"; "Smee, who was rather stupid."

facts.text: He treats dangers with odd, tactless cheer, calling the crocodile's pursuit a 'sort of a compliment' and bluntly noting the clock will one day run down and the crocodile will get Hook.
facts.argument: Smee: "in a way, it's sort of a compliment"; "Some day the clock will run down, and then he'll get you."

facts.text: Smee led the plan to maroon Tiger Lily on Marooners' Rock, ordering to hoist her onto it and leave her to drown.
facts.argument: "'Luff, you lubber,' cried an Irish voice that was Smee's... 'hoist the redskin on to it and leave her here to drown.'"

facts.text: Ignorant about what a 'mother' is; bluntly asks, "What's a mother?"
facts.argument: "What's a mother?" asked the ignorant Smee.

facts.text: Smee found and sat on the tom-tom, then beat it twice on Hook's order to fake an Indian victory; realizing the wickedness, he admired Hook more.
facts.argument: "Now Smee had found the tom-tom, and was at that moment sitting on it... Hook signed him to beat the tom-tom... Twice Smee beat upon the instrument... understanding of the dreadful wickedness... admired Hook so much."

facts.text: Aboard the Jolly Roger, Smee works the ship’s sewing machine, ever industrious and obliging; pathetically unaware of his own pathos, which can even move Hook to tears.
facts.argument: "the whir of the ship's sewing machine at which Smee sat, ever industrious and obliging ... pathetic Smee ... more than once on summer evenings he had touched the fount of Hook's tears and made it flow ... Smee was quite unconscious."

facts.text: Smee is perceived as lovable by the captured children aboard the Jolly Roger despite his threatening role; they clung to him even when he scolded and slapped them, and Michael tried on his spectacles.
facts.argument: "There was not a child on board the brig that night who did not already love him"; "they had only clung to him the more"; "Michael had tried on his spectacles"

facts.text: Smee tied Wendy to the mast and offered to save her if she would be his mother; she refused.
facts.argument: "It was Smee who tied her to the mast." "I'll save you if you promise to be my mother." ... She refused.

facts.text: Survives and later wanders the world wearing spectacles, making a living by claiming he was the only man Hook feared.
facts.argument: "Smee... wandered about the world in his spectacles, making a precarious living by saying he was the only man that Jas. Hook had feared."

summaries.text: Smee is the Irish boatswain of Hook's crew, oddly genial, known for stabbing "without offence," and the only Non-conformist among the pirates.

Smee is the genial Irish boatswain of Captain Hook's crew, known for his non-conformist attitude and odd behavior, like naming his cutlass "Johnny Corkscrew." He is characterized by his clumsiness and tendency to wipe his spectacles after a kill.

Smee is the clumsy Irish boatswain of Captain Hook's crew, known for his odd behavior, like naming his cutlass 'Johnny Corkscrew.' He is cheerful yet tactless, often oblivious to danger and his own pathos, which can even evoke sympathy from Hook.

Smee is the clumsy Irish boatswain of Captain Hook's crew, known for his cheerful yet tactless demeanor and odd habits, like naming his cutlass 'Johnny Corkscrew.' Despite his threatening role, he is perceived as lovable by the children aboard the Jolly Roger.

Smee is the clumsy Irish boatswain of Captain Hook's crew, known for his cheerful demeanor and odd habits, like naming his cutlass 'Johnny Corkscrew.' Despite his threatening role, he is perceived as lovable by the children aboard the Jolly Roger.

Smee is the clumsy Irish boatswain of Captain Hook's crew, known for his cheerful demeanor and odd habits, like naming his cutlass 'Johnny Corkscrew.' Despite his threatening role, he is perceived as lovable by the children aboard the Jolly Roger and is pathetically unaware of his own pathos.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "and Noodler, whose hands were fixed on backwards"

summaries.text: Noodler is a pirate in Hook's crew, distinguished by having hands fixed on backwards.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "and Robt. Mullins"

facts.text: Robert Mullins voiced pirate superstitions and jeered at the cloaked figure thought to be Wendy, hissing, "There's none can save you now, missy."
facts.argument: "'I've heard,' muttered Mullins, 'he always boards the pirate craft last'"; and later: "Mullins hissed jeeringly"

facts.text: Killed by Peter Pan during the battle aboard the Jolly Roger; Peter had just passed his sword through Mullins before challenging Hook.
facts.argument: "another, who had just passed his sword through Mullins, sprang into the fray"—the newcomer is revealed as Peter moments later.

summaries.text: Robert Mullins ("Robt. Mullins") is a pirate in Hook's crew, a ruffian known on the Spanish Main.

Robert Mullins, also known as "Robt. Mullins," is a notorious pirate in Hook's crew, recognized for his ruffian demeanor on the Spanish Main. He is known for voicing pirate superstitions and mocking Wendy, declaring, "There's none can save you now, missy."

Robert Mullins, aka "Robt. Mullins," is a notorious pirate in Hook's crew, known for his ruffian demeanor and mocking Wendy with, "There's none can save you now, missy." He was killed by Peter Pan during a battle aboard the Jolly Roger.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "and Alf Mason"

facts.text: Killed during the pirates’ ambush on Tiger Lily’s warriors; fell with Lean Wolf.
facts.argument: "with Lean Wolf fell Alf Mason, to disturb the Spanish Main no more"

summaries.text: Alf Mason is a pirate in Hook's crew, a ruffian long known on the Spanish Main.
Alf Mason is a notorious pirate in Hook's crew, recognized for his ruffian ways on the Spanish Main. He was killed during an ambush on Tiger Lily's warriors, falling alongside Lean Wolf.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "Bringing up the rear... comes Tiger Lily, proudly erect, a princess in her own right... the belle of the Piccaninnies, coquettish, cold and amorous by turns;... she staves off the altar with a hatchet."

facts.text: Brings up the rear of the war-party—the most dangerous position—proudly erect.
facts.argument: "Bringing up the rear, the place of greatest danger, comes Tiger Lily, proudly erect."

facts.text: Becomes Peter Pan's ally after he saves her life in the Mermaids' Lagoon.
facts.argument: “Peter saved Tiger Lily's life in the Mermaids' Lagoon, and so made her his ally.”

facts.text: Tiger Lily was captured boarding the pirate ship with a knife in her mouth; tied hand and foot, she was to be left on Marooners' Rock to drown, which she faced with the impassive pride of a chief's daughter.
facts.argument: "the third a captive... Tiger Lily... Her hands and ankles were tied... She was to be left on the rock to perish... They had caught her boarding the pirate ship with a knife in her mouth... she was the daughter of a chief."

facts.text: Escaped from the pirates at Mermaids' Lagoon after being freed due to Peter’s ruse.
facts.argument: "Smee... cut Tiger Lily's cords" and she "slid... into the water."

facts.text: Reaffirms loyalty to Peter, stating he saved her and vowing not to let pirates harm him.
facts.argument: "Me Tiger Lily... Peter Pan save me, me his velly nice friend. Me no let pirates hurt him."

facts.text: Survived the pirates’ ambush and escaped with a small remnant of her tribe thanks to Great Big Little Panther’s defense.
facts.argument: "cut a way through the pirates with Tiger Lily and a small remnant of the tribe."

summaries.text: Tiger Lily, the proud princess of the Piccaninny tribe, is known for her beauty and fierce nature. She leads the war-party's rear, a perilous position, and is notorious for fending off suitors with a hatchet.

Tiger Lily, the proud princess of the Piccaninny tribe, is known for her beauty and fierce nature. She leads the war-party's rear and becomes Peter Pan's ally after he saves her life in the Mermaids' Lagoon, famously fending off suitors with a hatchet.

Tiger Lily, the proud princess of the Piccaninny tribe, is known for her beauty and fierce nature. She becomes Peter Pan's ally after he saves her from drowning, bravely leading her war-party and fending off suitors with a hatchet.

Tiger Lily, the proud princess of the Piccaninny tribe, is known for her beauty and fierce spirit. After Peter Pan saves her from drowning, she becomes his loyal ally, leading her war-party and bravely defending against pirates and unwanted suitors.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "In the van, on all fours, is Great Big Little Panther, a brave of so many scalps that... they somewhat impede his progress."

facts.text: Cut a way through the pirates alongside Tiger Lily, enabling her and a small remnant of the tribe to escape.
facts.argument: "the terrible Panther... ultimately cut a way through the pirates with Tiger Lily and a small remnant of the tribe."

facts.text: Also referred to as "the terrible Panther" during this battle.
facts.argument: "Turley fell to the tomahawk of the terrible Panther"

summaries.text: Great Big Little Panther is a leading brave of the Piccaninny tribe, crawling in the van with so many scalps they hinder his movement.

Great Big Little Panther, also known as "the terrible Panther," is a brave of the Piccaninny tribe. He is notable for his bravery, having cut a path through pirates alongside Tiger Lily to help her and the tribe escape.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "comes the last figure of all, a gigantic crocodile. We shall see for whom she is looking presently."

facts.text: Joins the island's nocturnal procession as the last figure, a gigantic female crocodile seemingly hunting someone.
facts.argument: "comes the last figure of all, a gigantic crocodile... We shall see for whom she is looking presently. The crocodile passes, but soon the boys appear again."

facts.text: Swallowed a clock that makes it tick audibly and relentlessly follows Captain Hook after tasting his arm, seeking more.
facts.argument: "it swallowed a clock which goes tick tick inside it"; "it has followed me ever since... licking its lips for the rest of me."

facts.text: Serves as a timekeeper on the island; one can find it and wait for the clock inside it to strike.
facts.argument: "The way you got the time on the island was to find the crocodile, and then stay near him till the clock struck."

facts.text: Its audible ticking is used as a time reference by islanders, e.g., “ten o’clock by the crocodile.”
facts.argument: "It must have been not less than ten o'clock by the crocodile"

facts.text: Its internal clock had run down so it was not ticking; drawn by Peter’s imitation tick, it followed him toward the shore.
facts.argument: Peter "remembered that it had not been ticking... concluded rightly that the clock had run down... The crocodile was among those who heard the sound, and it followed him."

facts.text: Portrayed as a 'stupid beast,' a slave to a fixed idea, possibly mistaking Peter’s ticking for its own.
facts.argument: "Like slaves to a fixed idea, it was a stupid beast."

facts.text: Achieves its long-sought goal by devouring Captain Hook when he leaps into the sea.
facts.argument: "went content to the crocodile. Thus perished James Hook."

facts.text: Its ticking ceased at the end so Hook did not know it waited for him, enabling the fatal surprise.
facts.argument: "we purposely stopped the clock that this knowledge might be spared him"

summaries.text: The Crocodile is a gigantic female crocodile who participates in the island's nocturnal procession, appearing as the last figure and seemingly hunting someone.

The Crocodile is a gigantic female crocodile known for joining the island's nocturnal procession, appearing last and seemingly hunting. She audibly ticks after swallowing a clock and relentlessly pursues Captain Hook after tasting his arm.

The Crocodile is a gigantic female crocodile known for her relentless pursuit of Captain Hook after tasting his arm. She joins the island's nocturnal procession, audibly ticking after swallowing a clock, and serves as a timekeeper for the islanders.

The Crocodile is a gigantic female crocodile known for her relentless pursuit of Captain Hook after tasting his arm. She audibly ticks after swallowing a clock, serving as a timekeeper for the islanders and ultimately devours Hook, achieving her long-sought goal.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “You remember about her pet wolf… it very soon discovered that she had come to the island… After that it followed her about everywhere.”

summaries.text: Wendy’s devoted companion wolf in Neverland; upon discovering her arrival, it reunited with her and now follows her everywhere.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “Should we take the brush with the redskins at Slightly Gulch?”

summaries.text: A location in Neverland where the Lost Boys and the Redskins fought; notable as the scene showing Peter Pan’s habit of switching sides mid-fight.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “particularly of the Never bird that built in a tree overhanging the lagoon, and how the nest fell into the water, and still the bird sat on her eggs, and Peter gave orders that she was not to be disturbed.”

facts.text: Crossing the lagoon on her floating nest, she had learned to steer it with her wings; despite a short temper and language barrier, she came to save Peter and even abandoned her two eggs to give him the nest so he could drift ashore.
facts.argument: "By working her wings... she was able... to guide her strange craft"; "She had come to save him, to give him her nest, though there were eggs in it"; "deserting her eggs, so as to make her meaning clear."

facts.text: Her nest contained two large white eggs; after giving Peter the nest, she watched anxiously from above to see what he did with them, even covering her face with her wings and peeking.
facts.argument: "There were two large white eggs... The bird covered her face with her wings... but she could not help peeping between the feathers."

facts.text: She abandoned her original nest and adopted Starkey’s tarpaulin hat as a nest; this brimmed design later became the standard for all Never birds.
facts.argument: “She abandoned the nest… often Starkey… watched the bird sitting on his hat… all Never birds now build in that shape of nest, with a broad brim.”

summaries.text: A steadfast bird of Neverland who nested over the Mermaids’ Lagoon; when her nest fell into the water she remained on her eggs, and Peter ordered that she not be disturbed, after which she showed gratitude.

The Never Bird is a loyal bird from Neverland, known for nesting over Mermaids’ Lagoon. After her nest fell into the water, she selflessly gave it to Peter Pan, abandoning her two eggs. Despite her short temper, she anxiously watched over Peter's actions.

The Never Bird is a loyal, short-tempered bird from Neverland, known for nesting over Mermaids’ Lagoon. She selflessly gave her nest, containing two eggs, to Peter Pan and anxiously watched over him, later adopting Starkey’s hat as her new nest.

Marooners' Rock is a small outcrop in Mermaids' Lagoon, a resting spot for Wendy and the boys. It serves as a meeting place for Peter Pan and the mermaids, but is also a sinister location where evil captains maroon victims at high tide.

No. 14, the Darling family's home, is a nurturing nursery where the children return to ensure their parents stay in for the evening. It symbolizes warmth and care, featuring key events like Peter Pan and Tinker Bell tricking Wendy at the window.

No. 14, the Darling family's nurturing nursery, symbolizes warmth and care. Key events include Peter Pan and Tinker Bell tricking Wendy at the window. After Nana's passing, it becomes Jane's nursery, retaining only two beds and losing the kennel.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Introduced as Wendy’s daughter, born years after Wendy grows up and marries.

facts.text: She has an odd, inquiring look and asks questions mostly about Peter Pan; she loves to hear stories about Peter from Wendy in the old nursery.
facts.argument: “She was called Jane, and always had an odd inquiring look… When she was old enough… they were mostly about Peter Pan. She loved to hear of Peter, and Wendy told her… in the very nursery…”

facts.text: At bedtime she invents raising a sheet as a tent for story time and now knows the story of Peter’s visit better than Wendy, prompting exact lines.
facts.argument: "It was Jane's invention to raise the sheet..."; "You have missed a bit," ... "who now knows the story better than her mother."

facts.text: She feels attuned to Peter’s crow—often hearing it in her sleep—and can imitate it more accurately than Wendy.
facts.argument: "I often hear it when I am sleeping," Jane said... "No, it wasn't... it was like this;" and she did it ever so much better than her mother.

facts.text: Among Neverland places, she prefers the home under the ground and wishes she were "gay and innocent and heartless" like those who can fly.
facts.argument: "I think I liked the home under the ground best of all."; "I do wish I were gay and innocent and heartless."

facts.text: Jane awakens to Peter’s sobs, shows immediate interest, addresses him as “Boy,” and meets him formally with exchanged bows.
facts.argument: “She sat up in bed, and was interested at once. ‘Boy,’ she said… Peter… bowed to her, and she bowed… ‘My name is Peter Pan.’”

facts.text: Becomes Peter's 'mother' and flies with him to Neverland for spring cleaning; flying quickly becomes her easiest way of moving; later she grows up and has a daughter, Margaret.

facts.evidence: "Wendy's began to be scrawled all over with him." / "Yes, he is rather cocky," Wendy admitted. / "He is Peter Pan, you know, mother."

facts.text: Wendy reports Peter’s nocturnal visits: he sits on her bed and plays pipes; she considers him her size and not grown up.
facts.evidence: 'sat on the foot of her bed and played on his pipes'; 'he isn't grown up… just my size.'

facts.text: Wendy sews Peter’s detached shadow back onto his foot.

facts.text: Peter knelt by Wendy, called the protective button his ‘kiss,’ and begged her to get better so he could show her the mermaids.

facts.evidence: "Please, sir... a lady lies very ill"; "Wendy, sing the kind of house you would like to have."

facts.text: Peter insists the boys need a nice motherly person and supports Wendy taking on the role; Wendy agrees to be their mother.
facts.evidence: Peter: "What we need is just a nice motherly person." Wendy: "Very well... I will do my best."

facts.text: Peter and Wendy collaborated to invent a new game of pretending not to have adventures.
